Gentlemen :

This refers to your letter requesting for a tax exemption certification by way of confirmatory ruling pursuant to Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 72-2003 and Presidential Decree (PD) No. 269. HTcADC

It is represented that Leyte II Electric Cooperative, Inc. (LEYECO II) with Tax Identification Number (TIN) 000-000-000-000 is registered with the National Electrification Administration (NEA) as a non-stock, non-profit membership electric cooperative bearing Certification No. 71, issued on October 26, 1975; that it is formed primarily for the purpose of supplying, promoting and encouraging the fullest use of electric service to its members on an "area coverage."

In reply, please be informed that Section 39 of PD No. 269 provides:

"Section 39. Assistance to Cooperatives; Exemption from Taxes, Imposts, Duties, Fees; Assistance from the National Power Corporation. Pursuant to the national policy declared in Section 2, the Congress hereby finds and declares that the following assistance to cooperative is necessary and appropriate:

(a) Provided that it operates in conformity with the purposes and provisions of this Decree, cooperative (1) shall be permanently exempt from paying income taxes, and (2) for a period ending on December 31; of the thirtieth full calendar year after the date of a cooperative's organization or conversion hereunder, or until it shall become completely free of indebtedness incurred by borrowing, whichever event first occurs, shall be exempt from the payment (a) of all National Government, local government and municipal taxes and fees, including franchise, filing, recordation, license or permit fees or taxes and any fees, charges, or costs involved in any court or administrative proceeding in which it may be a party, and (b) of all duties or imposts on foreign goods acquired for its operations, the period of such exemption for a new cooperative formed by consolidation, as provided for in Section 29, to begin from as of the date of the beginning of such period for the constituent consolidating cooperative which was most recently organized or converted under this Decree: x x x"

On October 10, 1984, PD No. 1955 was enacted by then President Ferdinand E. Marcos. It withdrew all exemptions or any preferential treatment in the payment of duties, taxes, fees, imposts, and other charges granted to private business enterprises and/or persons engaged in any economic activity. CAIHTE

On January 8, 1986, PD No. 2008 was issued, requiring the Minister of Finance to immediately restore the tax exemption of all electric cooperatives. However, in December 1986, then Pres. Corazon C. Aquino issued Executive Order (EO) No. 93 which withdrew all tax and duty exemptions granted to private entities effective March 10, 1987. But Memorandum Order No. 65, dated January 23, 1987, suspended the implementation of the said EO until June 30, 1987 for cooperatives. Effective July 1, 1987, Fiscal Incentives Regulatory Board (FIRB) No. 24-87 restored the tax and duty exemption privileges of electric cooperatives under PD No. 269. FIRB Resolution No. 24-87 reads:

"BE IT RESOLVED, as it is hereby resolved, That the tax and duty exemption privileges of electric cooperatives granted under the terms and conditions of Presidential Decree No. 269 (creating the National Electrification Administration as a corporation, prescribing its powers and activities, appropriating the necessary funds therefore and declaring a national policy objective for the total electrification of the Philippines on an area coverage basis; the organization, promotion and development of electric cooperatives to attain the said objective, prescribing terms and conditions for their operations, the repeal of Republic Act No. 6038, and for other purposes), as amended, are restored effective July 1, 1987: Provided, however, That income from their electric service operations and other sources including the interest income from bank deposits and yield or any other monetary benefit from bank deposits and yield or any other similar arrangements shall remain taxable: x x x"

Based on the foregoing, while FIRB Resolution No. 24-87 restored the duty and tax exemptions enjoyed by Electric Cooperatives established pursuant to PD No. 269 (Sec. 39), said Resolution, however, expressly provides that "income from their electric service operations and other sources including the interest income from bank deposits and yield or any other monetary benefit from bank deposits and yield or any other similar arrangements shall remain taxable." Thus, this Office opines that LEYECO II's income from its electric service operations is now subject to income tax pursuant to said FIRB Resolution No. 24-87.

Beginning January 1, 2006, LEYECO II is subject to all other national government taxes and fees, including VAT, filing, recordation, license or permit fees or taxes as its exemption ended on December 31, 2005, the thirtieth full calendar year after the date of the cooperative's organization [1] as stated in its registration papers or until it shall become completely free of indebtedness incurred by borrowing, whichever event comes first. (BIR Ruling No. 398-2013 dated November 4, 2013)

Moreover, all Electric Cooperatives registered with the NEA, shall be subject to the following:

1. 20% final income tax on interest from any currency bank deposit and yield or any other monetary benefit from deposit substitutes and from trust funds and similar arrangements and royalties derived from sources within the Philippines;

2. 15% final income tax on interest income derived from a depositary bank under the expanded foreign currency deposit system; aScITE

3. Capital Gains Tax on sales or exchanges of real property classified as capital assets or shares of stock not listed in the local stock exchange;

4. Documentary stamp taxes on transactions of cooperatives dealing with non-members, except transactions with banks and insurance companies; Provided that whenever one party to the taxable document enjoys the exemption from DST, the other party who is not exempt shall be the one directly liable for the tax;

5. VAT billed on purchases of goods and services;

6. Value-Added Tax, on sales relative to the generation and distribution of electricity as well as their importation of machineries and equipment, including spare parts, which shall be directly used in the generation and distribution of electricity; and

7. All other taxes for which the ECs are not otherwise expressly exempted by any law.

Upon the effectivity of R.A. No. 9337, the exemption from VAT of electric cooperatives was removed. Consequently, Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 16-2005, as amended by RR No. 4-2007, particularly Section 4.108-2 (13) and Section 4.108-3 (f) provide that sales of electricity by generation, transmission, and/or distribution companies are now subject to 12% VAT on their gross receipts. Provided, however, that sale of power or fuel generated through renewable sources of energy such as, but not limited to, biomass, solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, ocean energy, and other emerging energy sources using technologies such as fuel cells and hydrogen fuels shall be subject to 0% VAT.

Therefore, electric cooperatives are now also subject to VAT on their gross receipts pursuant to R.A. No. 9337, as implemented by RR No. 16-2005, as amended.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void. DETACa

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

1. LEYECO II was organized on October 26, 1975, hence, the exemption granted under PD 269 already ended on December 31, 2005 which is December 31 of the thirtieth full calendar year after the date of its organization.

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request on behalf of your client the PUBLIC INVESTMENT FUND ("PIF") for confirmation that the income derived by its subsidiaries, The Saudi Second Investment Company ("SSIC") and The Saudi Fourth Investment Company ("SFIC") (hereafter collectively referred as the "Companies"), from its investments in the Philippines in stocks, bonds or other domestic securities are exempt from income tax. HEITAD

Background

1. The SSIC and SFIC are single person limited liability companies incorporated in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia ("the Kingdom" or "KSA") wholly owned by the PIF. The PIF is the sovereign wealth fund of the government established in the KSA. PIF was formed by Royal Decree in 1971 (hereafter the "Decree") and is now regulated by the 2019 Law of PIF (hereafter the "Law").

2. In accordance with the Decree and Law, PIF is not a separate corporate entity and does not issue shares or any transferable interest.

3. Effectively, the Decree states that PIF has a "public legal personality," referring to an entity/authority in KSA that is an integral part of the KSA. PIF has a Governor with a rank of Minister that is responsible for looking after the day-to-day aspects of PIF's operations (the Governor reports to the Board of PIF). In that respect, PIF is similar to ministries where ministers look after day-to-day operational aspects and report to the KSA.

4. PIF does not pay income tax [that is imposed primarily on non-Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC) interest in KSA entities] and Zakat (which is a religious levy imposed primarily on GCC interest in KSA entities). PIF is considered as tax resident in the KSA.

5. Given that PIF is an integral part of the KSA, its earnings are distributed to the Treasury of the sovereign/Ministry of Finance of the KSA. Hence, no portion of the earnings of PIF inures any benefit to any "private person."

6. The SSIC and SFIC were formed pursuant to the Company Law of the Kingdom promulgated by Royal Decree No. M/3 dated 28/01/1437H. The Companies are wholly owned by PIF. aDSIHc

7. The Companies' purpose is to invest its funds (provided by the PIF) in shares, bonds and other securities and to invest in portfolios, funds and regional and global stock exchanges and financial markets, with the PIF as the ultimate beneficial owner. The Companies are likewise managed by the PIF. Particularly, they are under the oversight of the PIF governor, Yasir Al-Rumayyan.

8. Such Companies are separate legal entities and taxpayers but rely on third party service providers and PIF's staff to execute certain tasks on behalf of such Companies. Like PIF, such Companies never engage in day-to-day operations of the investee companies, but merely exercise shareholder level functions based on the governance of such investee companies. Thus, their activities are clearly limited to investment and not commercial/trading activities.

9. These Companies are incorporated for various policy, legal, regulatory, commercial or contracting reasons where PIF's direct engagement was either not feasible or could put PIF into a less favorable position. The Companies are 100% owned by PIF. In this respect, such Companies are functional extension of PIF itself and should be clearly distinguished from other commercial or trading subsidiaries that PIF owns for the purposes of this analysis (for the avoidance of doubt, such commercial subsidiaries are also autonomous in their own right, e.g., have separate commercial mandate/activities, separate governance, independent boards and day-to-day management teams, etc.)

10. The Companies currently intend to invest in listed shares of Philippine domestic corporations.

Discussion/Ruling

Section 32 (B) (7) (a) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, which you invoke as basis of exemption from payment of Philippine income tax and withholding tax on income that the Companies will receive should they invest in the Philippines, provides:

"(B) Exclusions from Gross Income. — The following items shall not be included in gross income and shall be exempt from taxation under this Title:

xxx xxx xxx

(7) Miscellaneous Items. —

(a) Income Derived by Foreign Government. — Income derived from investments in the Philippines in loans, stocks, bonds or other domestic securities, or from interest on deposits in banks in the Philippines by (i) foreign governments, (ii) financing institutions owned, controlled, or enjoying refinancing from foreign governments, and (iii) international or regional financial institutions established by foreign governments."

In relation thereto, "financing companies" is defined as follows:

"2.7. Financing Companies. — shall refer to corporations except banks, investment houses, savings and loan associations, insurance companies, cooperatives, and other financial institutions organized or operating under other special laws, which are primarily organized for the purpose of extending credit facilities to consumers and to industrial, commercial, or agricultural enterprises, by direct lending or by discounting or factoring commercial papers or accounts receivables, or by buying and selling contracts, leases, chattel mortgages, or other evidences of indebtedness, or by financial leasing of movable as well as immovable properties (R.A. No. 5980, as amended by R.A. No. 8556)." [1]

Based on the representations made, it would appear that the Companies do not fall under any of the above enumeration. Even though their investor is comprised of a foreign government, it is not an institution contemplated under Section 32 (B) (7) (a) of the Tax Code, as amended. The exemption covers income derived by financing institutions either owned, controlled, or enjoying refinancing from foreign governments, or those which are established by foreign governments. Records do not even show that the Companies are financial institutions in contemplation of law rather they are investment companies. Under Section 4 of Republic Act (RA) No. 2629, or the Investment Company Act, an investment company is incorporated for the primary purpose of investing, reinvesting, or trading in securities. The Articles of Association of the Companies state that they have been formed to purchase and own shares, stocks and assets in companies inside and outside the KSA, to invest their funds in shares, sukuk, bonds and other securities and to invest in portfolios, funds and regional and global stock exchanges and financial markets. Considering that the Companies are performing investment activities, they are classified as investment companies pursuant to RA No. 2629. ATICcS

In this case, the Companies are just ordinary private companies which happen to be managed and administered by a financing institution controlled by a foreign government. They are not financing institutions owned, controlled, or enjoying refinancing from a foreign government. The Companies are mere investee companies with respect to the financing institution, PIF, and consequently, to the foreign government.

IN VIEW OF THE FOREGOING, this Office hereby rules that the Companies are not considered as financing institutions within the purview of Section 32 (B) (7) (a) (ii) of the Tax Code, as amended, hence, income that will be earned should the Companies invest in the Philippines in loans, stocks, bonds or other domestic securities, or from interest on deposits in banks in the Philippines shall be subject to Philippine income tax and withholding taxes.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request on behalf of your client, Sunjin Philippines Corporation and Sunjin Genetics Corporation ("Sunjin Corporations"), for partial reconsideration of BIR Ruling No. 312-2017 dated December 11, 2017, by deleting the prohibition which states that a "trustee should not in any way use the retirement fund to invest/deposit in any of the employer's business ventures because it would destroy the separate entity of the trust."

Under BIR Ruling No. 312-2017, the Bureau finds Sunjin Multiemployer Contribution Plan to be a "reasonable retirement plan" within the contemplation of Section 32 (B) (6) (a) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended ("Tax Code"). Therefore, the: (a) retirement benefits that will be received by a qualified retiring employee-member shall be exempt from income tax provided that he/she: (i) had been in the service of the same private firm for at least ten (10) years; and (ii) is already fifty (50) years old at the time of retirement; (b) income of the trust fund from its investments is exempt from income tax; and (c) contributions of the company to the retirement fund are deductible from its gross income. One of the conditions stated in BIR Ruling No. 312-2017 is that the trustee should not in any way use the retirement fund to invest/deposit in any of the employer's business ventures because it would destroy the separate entity of the trust. ETHIDa

In reply, please be informed that an employees' trust (the "Retirement Fund") is a trust maintained by an employer to provide retirement, pension or other benefits to its employees. It bears emphasis that the Retirement Fund, which is governed by an employer-appointed trustee, is a taxable entity separate from the employer. [1]

Section 5 of Revenue Regulations ("RR") No. 1-68, as amended, provides that the Retirement Fund may be used to purchase investments subject to specific exceptions, to wit:

"SECTION 5. Investment. — No specific limitations are provided in the law with respect to investments which may be made by the trustees of an employee's trust. Generally, the fund may be used by the trustees to purchase any investments permitted by the trust agreement. However, the exemption of the trust income under Section 60 (b) of the Tax Code, may be denied if the trust —

(a) lends any part of its income or corpus without adequate security and a reasonable rate of interest;

(b) pays any compensation in excess of a reasonable allowance for salaries or other compensation for personal services actually rendered;

(c) makes any part of its services available on a preferential basis;

(d) makes any substantial purchase of securities or any other property for more than adequate consideration in money or money's worth;

(e) sells any substantial part of its securities or other property, for less than an adequate consideration in money or money's worth; or

(f) engages in any other transaction which results in a substantial diversion of its income or corpus.

to or from the employer or, if the employer is an individual, to or from a member of the family of the employer, or to or from a corporation controlled by the employer through the ownership, directly or indirectly, of 50% or more of the total combined voting power of all classes of stock entitled to vote or 50% or more of the total value of shares of all classes of stock of the corporation." (Underscoring supplied) TIADCc

Corollarily, Section 60 (B) of the Tax Code provides that any income derived by Retirement Fund shall not be subject to income tax as long as, among others, all its income will be used exclusively for the benefit of such employees, without any diversion towards alternative objectives, to wit:

"SECTION 60. Imposition of Tax. —

(A) x x x

(B) Exception. The tax imposed by this Title shall not apply to employee's trust which forms part of the pension, stock bonus or profit-sharing plan of an employer for the benefit of some or all of his employees (1) if contributions are made to the trust by such employer, or employees, or both for the purpose of distributing to such employees the earnings and principal of the fund accumulated by the trust in accordance with such plan, and (2) if under the trust instrument it is impossible, at any time prior to the satisfaction of liabilities with respect to employees under the trust, for any part of the corpus or income be (within the taxable year or thereafter) used for, or diverted to, purposes other than the exclusive benefit of his employees: Provided, That any amount actually distributed to any employee or distributee shall be taxable to him in the year in which so distributed to the extent that it exceeds the amount contributed by such employee or distributee"

Based on the foregoing provisions, while it is true that there are no specific limitations provided in the law with respect to investments which may be made by the trustee of a Retirement Fund, it is important however, that the said fund be invested in proper and sound investments for the sole benefit of the employees. Also, by removing the income tax exemption of Retirement Fund income relating to transactions listed in Section 5 of RR No. 1-68, it may be deduced that the intention of the Legislature is to ensure that the trustee will only invest the Retirement Fund in income-generating investments, thereby guaranteeing that the Retirement Fund will always be sufficient to pay for the retirement benefits of any qualified retiring employee. cSEDTC

Section 5 (f) of RR No. 1-68 specifically states that the trustee of the Retirement Fund is prohibited to engage in other transactions with the employer which may result in a substantial diversion of its income or corpus. Considering the potential variability in the business operations of the employer which may adversely affect its capability to contribute to the Retirement Fund, it is deemed best to allow the trustees of a Retirement Fund to use and/or invest said funds in various diverse investments (other than the business ventures of the employer) with the sole objective of accumulating adequate resources to fulfill its obligations. Therefore, permitting the trustee to invest the Retirement Fund in the business ventures of the employer runs contrary to the aforementioned principle and may result in the inability to meet the Retirement Fund's obligations.

Furthermore, aside from the above-stated rationale, the prohibition to use the Retirement Fund to invest/deposit in any of the employer's business ventures is to maintain the separation of funds (or avoid the comingling of funds) of the Retirement Fund from those of the employer, which may be an avenue for evasion of taxes. [2]

Such being the case, this Office hereby rules that your request for partial reconsideration of BIR Ruling No. 312-2017 dated December 11, 2017, by deleting the prohibition to use the retirement fund to invest/deposit in any of the employer's business ventures, is denied for bereft of merit. Consider this as our final resolution on the matter.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request for a ruling that your importation of various products consisting of beverages are exempt from the payment of excise tax imposed on sweetened beverages under Republic Act (RA) No. 10963, otherwise known as the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion (TRAIN) Law. AIDSTE

It is represented that you already paid the excise taxes due on the importation of your products (sweetened beverages) to facilitate the immediate release from the Bureau of Customs (BOC) subject to the final determination that said products are exempt from the payment of excise tax; that you were advised by the BOC to obtain from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) a Certification that your products subject of various Authority to Release Imported Goods are excluded from the imposition of excise tax; and that you were able to secure a Certification from the FDA that your products are not covered by the TRAIN Law.

In reply, please be informed that Section 47 of RA No. 10963, provides, viz.:

"SEC. 47. A new section designated as Section 150-B under Chapter VI, Title VI of the NIRC, as amended, is hereby inserted to read as follows:

SEC. 150-B. Sweetened Beverages. —

(A) Rate and Base of Tax. — Effective January 1, 2018:

(1) A tax of Six pesos (P6.00) per liter of volume capacity shall be levied, assessed, and collected on sweetened beverages using purely caloric sweeteners, and purely non-caloric sweeteners, or a mix of caloric and non-caloric sweeteners: Provided, That this rate shall not apply to sweetened beverages using high fructose corn syrup: Provided, further, That sweetened beverages using purely coconut sap sugar and purely steviol glycosides shall be exempt from this tax;" (Underscoring ours)

In relation thereto, Section 3 of Revenue Regulations No. 20-2018, implementing the imposition of excise tax on sweetened beverages pursuant to Section 47 of RA No. 10963 provides, to wit:

"SECTION 3. Tax Rates and Bases. — There shall be levied, assessed and collected, effective January 1, 2018, a specific tax on sweetened beverages, in accordance with the following:

PRODUCT DESCRIPTION

Tax Rate
(per liter of volume capacity)

Using purely caloric sweeteners, and purely non-caloric sweeteners, or a mix of caloric and non-caloric sweeteners

P6.00

Using purely high fructose corn syrup or in combination with any caloric or non-caloric sweetener

P12.00

Using purely coconut sap sugar and purely steviol glycosides

Exempt

From the afore-quoted provisions, [1] it is clear that only those sweetened beverages using purely coconut sap sugar and purely steviol glycosides shall be exempt from excise tax. Thus, sweetened beverages although without added caloric and non-caloric sweeteners are still subject to excise tax if the same contain purely high fructose corn syrup. SDAaTC

Furthermore, in a letter addressed to Fly Ace Corporation's Import and Regulatory Manager dated April 26, 2018, the FDA certified that per its CFRR record, the following FDA-registered products have no added caloric and non-caloric sweetener, but without mentioning whether the following products do not contain purely high fructose corn syrup:

1. Mott's Apple Juice — Juice from Concentrate with Added Vitamin C — Original

2. 100% Apple Juice Original — Juice from Concentrate with Added Vitamin C

3. Old Orchard 100% Apple Juice from Concentrate

4. Old Orchard Organic 100% Juice Apple

5. Rauch Happy Day Apple Juice

6. Rauch Happy Day Orange Juice

7. Rauch Apple Juice

8. Rauch Orange Juice

9. Rauch Happy Day 100% Multivitamin Juice from Concentrate and Puree Concentrate with 9 Vitamins

10. Jolly Fresh Apple Juice from Concentrate

11. Jolly Fresh Orange Juice from Concentrate

12. May 100% Sparkling Red Grape Juice

13. May 100% Sparkling White Grape Juice

14. Welch's Family Farmer Owned® 100% Grape Juice from Concentrate with Added Ingredients, 120% Vitamin C

15. Welch's Grape Juice with Fiber

16. Welch's Grape Juice with Calcium

17. Jolly Fresh 100% Prune Juice

In view of the foregoing, this Office regrets to inform you that your request cannot be granted for lack of factual and legal basis. Thus, the above-stated FDA-registered products (sweetened beverages) are subject to excise tax imposed under Section 47 of RA No. 10963. AaCTcI

Please be guided accordingly.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request for a ruling on whether the reconveyance of a parcel of land without consideration is exempt from creditable withholding tax (CWT), and documentary stamp tax (DST). EcTCAD

It is represented that on June 17, 2022, a Deed of Sale was entered into between BBB married to CCC (Owners) and Cityland Development Corporation (Cityland), wherein the latter purchased from the former a parcel of land with an area of 2,625 square meters (sqm.), more or less, excluding the existing improvements thereon, identified as Lot No. 12-A-2-A of the subdivision plan (LRC) PSD-316369, being a portion of Lot 12-A-2 (LRC) PSD-305660, situated in Brgy. Santolan now under Brgy. Dela Paz, Pasig City and covered by Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) No. (PT-115090) 011-2022001618 (subject property). [1] It was subsequently discovered that a 56.98 sqm. portion of the subject property was affected by the overlapping of the structures of the adjacent lot (excluded area).

As a consequence thereof, Cityland deducted from the total purchase price the amount equivalent to the excluded area from the subject property. Moreover, the excluded area was segregated from the subject property and thereafter reconvened to the Owners without any consideration as per Deed of Reconveyance dated July 11, 2023 (subject transaction).

From the foregoing, you are of the opinion that the subject transaction is not subject to CGT under Section 24 (D) (1) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, there being no consideration to the reconveyance. You are likewise of the opinion that the subject transaction is not subject to CWT and DST prescribed in Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 2-98, as amended and Section 196 of the Tax Code, as amended.

In reply, please be informed that this Office is constrained to not subscribe to your opinion towards the taxability of the subject transaction. The Tax Code, as amended, does not define nor qualify the phrase "transfer," thus, it must be applied without attempted or strained interpretation. It shall be construed in its plain and simple meaning. The word "transferencia" (transfer) is defined by the "Diccionario de la Academia de la Lengua Castellana" as "accion y efecto de transferir" (the act and effect of transferring); and the verb "transferir," as "ceder o renunciar en otro el derecho o dominio que se tiene sobre una cosa, haciendole dueno de ella" (to assign or waive the right in, or absolute ownership of, a thing in favor of another, making him the owner thereof). The word "transfer" is defined as follows: Transfer means any act by which property of one person is vested in another. [2]

The subject transaction, not being categorically exempt from, or subject to another tax treatment pursuant to provisions of the Tax Code, as amended, or other special tax laws, is therefore considered taxable notwithstanding its lack of consideration. SDHTEC

From the foregoing, the statutory taxpayer in the subject transaction is evidently Cityland. Accordingly, being an entity engaged in real estate business, the reconveyance of the excluded area by Cityland is considered a transfer of ordinary asset pursuant to the provisions of RR No. 7-2003, [3] thus, subject to corporate income tax and value-added tax pursuant to Sections 27 (A) and, 105 to 106 of the Tax Code, as amended.

Consequently, the owners are likewise bound by Section 2.57.2 (F) of RR No. 2-98, as amended, viz.:

"SEC. 2.57.2. Income Payments Subject to Creditable Withholding Tax and Rates Prescribed Thereon. — Except as herein otherwise provided, there shall be withheld a creditable income tax at the rates herein specified for each class of payee from the following items of income payments to persons residing in the Philippines:

xxx xxx xxx

(F) Gross selling price or total amount of consideration or its equivalent paid to the seller/owner for the sale, exchange, or transfer of real property classified as ordinary asset. — A creditable withholding tax based on the gross selling price/total amount of consideration or the fair market value determined in accordance with Section 6(E) of the Code, whichever is higher, paid to the seller/owner for the sale, transfer or exchange of real property, other than capital asset, shall be imposed upon the withholding agent/buyer, in accordance with the following schedule:

xxx xxx xxx

B. Upon the following values of real property, where the seller/transferor is habitually engaged in the real estate business:

With a selling price of Five Hundred Thousand Pesos (P500,000.00) or less — 1.5%

With a selling price of more than Five Hundred Thousand Pesos (P500,000.00) but not more than Two Million Pesos (P2,000,000.00) — 3.0%

With a selling price of more than Two Million Pesos (P2,000,000.00) — 5.0%

xxx xxx xxx

Gross selling price shall mean the consideration stated in the sales document or the fair market value determined in accordance with Section 6 (E) of the Code, whichever is higher. x x x

If the buyer is an individual not engaged in trade or business, the following rules shall apply:

xxx xxx xxx

(ii) If, on the other hand, the sale is on a 'cash basis' or is a 'deferred-payment sale not in the installment plan' (that is, payments in the year of sale exceed 25% of the selling price), the buyer shall withhold the tax based on the gross selling price or fair market value of the property, whichever is higher, on the first installment."

Furthermore, the subject transaction, being a disposition of real property under the Tax Code, as amended, is likewise subject to the documentary stamp tax (DST) imposed in Section 196 of the same Code. HSAcaE

Please be guided accordingly.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request on behalf of your client, Julie's Franchise Corporation (JFC), for confirmation that:

1. The franchise fees received by JFC are subject to twenty-five percent (25%) regular corporate income tax and not to the twenty percent (20%) final withholding tax (FWT) on royalties and other passive income; and

2. The franchise fees are subject to the expanded withholding tax (EWT) of two percent (2%) if the franchisee/payor belongs to the top 20,000 corporations by the Bureau.

Background:

1. JFC is a domestic corporation duly organized and existing under and by virtue of the laws of the Republic of the Philippines and registered with the: (a) Securities and Exchange Commission with Company Registration Number No. C199800576; [1] and (b) Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) with Taxpayer Identification Number 000-000-000-000. AScHCD

2. JFC is engaged in franchising business and, in relation thereto, one of its primary purposes is to conduct, carry on and deal in the business of acquiring, developing, managing and utilizing any and all tradenames, trademarks, service marks, brand names, copyrights, patents, charters, goodwill, master franchises and licenses, including other intellectual property rights, necessary to commence and operate the relevant business enterprise, as well as to grant, issue, allow, permit, authorize, sanction and accredit the use, employment, exploitation and availment of such tradenames, trademarks service marks, brand names, copyrights, patents, charters, goodwill, master franchises and licenses and other intellectual property rights, for and in consideration of the payment of fees, dividends, royalties, charges, dues, commissions and remunerations, and in connection therewith, to set up, create and establish management services, techniques, technologies and networks for the expansion of the business enterprises relating to the acquisition, development, management and utilization of tradenames, trademarks, service marks, brand names, copyrights, patents, charters, goodwill, master franchises and licenses and other intellectual property rights (the Primary Purpose). [2]

3. JFC owns the valuable trademark, service mark, and tradename "Julie's Bakeshop" in addition to various trademarks, service marks, trade names, mascots, slogans, designs, insignias, emblems, symbols, package designs, distinctive building designs, and architectural features, logos, and other propriety identifying characteristics; and a distinctive system for merchandising its products through the operation of Julie's Bakeshop (collectively, the Systems and Marks). HESIcT

4. JFC has existing Franchise Agreements with BBB, [3] CCC, [4] and DDD, [5] (collectively, the Franchisees) for the grant of a non-exclusive license to construct, own and operate a Julie's Bakeshop and to use the System and Marks of JFC in the operation of the said Franchise.

5. Under the Franchise Agreements, JFC, among others: (a) retains all rights with respect to the operation of Julie's Bakeshops as well as the relating Systems and Marks; [6] (b) shall conduct training programs for the franchisees and their respective personnel; [7] and (c) at its option, make available to or specify for Franchisee an applicable software license for computer software packages designed and developed for the system by JFC or on its behalf. [8]

6. For the licensing of its operations, JFC is paid a franchise fee in the amount of PhP168,000.00 inclusive of 12% value-added tax and a continuing license fee of five percent (5%) based on Franchisees' gross sales (the Royalty Fees). [9]

In reply, please be informed that Section 27 (D) (1) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended (Tax Code) provides that royalties received by domestic corporations from sources within the Philippines shall be subject to FWT at the rate of twenty percent (20%), to wit:

"SEC. 27. Rates of Income tax on Domestic Corporations. —

xxx xxx xxx

(D) Rates of Tax on Certain Passive Incomes. —

(1) Interest from Deposits and Yield or any other Monetary Benefit from Deposit Substitutes and from Trust Funds and Similar Arrangements, and Royalties. — A final tax at the rate of twenty percent (20%) is hereby imposed upon the amount of interest on currency bank deposit and yield or any other monetary benefit from deposit substitutes and from trust funds and similar arrangements received by domestic corporations, and royalties, derived from sources within the Philippines. x x x" (Underscoring supplied)

Section 42 (A) (4) of the Tax Code provides that royalties received from the following transactions shall be treated as gross income from sources within the Philippines:

"SEC. 42. Income from Sources Within the Philippines. —

(A) Gross Income from Sources Within the Philippines. — The following items of gross income shall be treated as gross income from sources within the Philippines:

xxx xxx xxx

(4) Rentals and Royalties. — Rentals and royalties from property located in the Philippines or from any interest in such property, including rentals or royalties for —

(a) The use of or the right or privileges to use in the Philippines any copyright, patent, design or model, plan, secret formula or process, goodwill, trademark, trade brand or other like property or right;

(b) The use of, or the right to use in the Philippines any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment;

(c) The supply of scientific, technical, industrial or commercial knowledge or information;

(d) The supply of any assistance that is ancillary and subsidiary to, and is furnished as a means of enabling the application or enjoyment of, any such property or right as is mentioned in paragraph (a), any such equipment as is mentioned in paragraph (b) or any such knowledge or information as is mentioned in paragraph (c); x x x." (Underscoring supplied)

Based on the foregoing provisions, it is clear that to be subject to the twenty percent (20%) FWT, the royalties must be in the nature of passive income as defined in Section 42 (A) (4) of the Tax Code. [10] Otherwise, said income shall be considered as ordinary or taxable income subject to the regular income tax rate of: (a) thirty percent (30%) for income earned before July 1, 2020; or (b) twenty-five percent (25%) for income earned after July 1, 2020 pursuant to Section 27 (A) of the Tax Code. AcICHD

In the case of Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Shinko Electric Industries Co., Ltd., [11] citing the case of Chamber of Real Estate and Builders Associations, Inc. vs. The Honorable Executive Secretary Alberto Romulo, et al., [12] the Supreme Court explained that passive income refers to those income that is not generated in the active pursuit and performance of the corporation's primary purpose but arises from the company's assets. Therefore, such passive income is subject to final taxes and not covered by regular income tax.

Applied in this case, documents show that the Royalty Fees received by JFC from its Franchisees by virtue of its Franchise Agreements refer to income generated by JFC from activities that are in accordance with its Primary Purpose. Accordingly, such Royalty Fees are considered income generated in the active pursuit and performance of JFC's business, and therefore are classified as ordinary business income subject to regular corporate income tax.

Such being the case, this Office hereby rules that the Royalty Fees received by JFC from its Franchisees are not passive income subject to the twenty percent (20%) FWT but are considered ordinary or taxable income subject to the regular income tax rate of (a) thirty percent (30%) for income earned before July 1, 2020; or (b) twenty-five percent (25%) for income earned after July 1, 2020. caITAC

On the issue on the applicable withholding tax rate, please be informed that Section 2.57.2 (I) of RR No. 2-98, as amended, [13] states that:

"Section 2.57.2. Income Payments subject to Creditable Withholding Tax and Rates prescribed thereon. —

xxx xxx xxx

(I) Income payment made by top withholding agents, either private corporations or individuals, to their local/resident supplier of goods and local/resident supplier of services other than those covered by other rates of withholding tax. [formerly under letters (M) and (W)] — Income payments made by any of the top withholding agents, as determined by the Commissioner, to their local/resident supplier of goods/services, including non-resident aliens engaged in trade or business in the Philippines, shall be subjected to the following withholding tax rates:

Supplier of goods — One percent (1%)

Supplier of services — Two percent (2%)"

Based on the foregoing, if the payor of the Royalty Fees is one of the top withholding agents as determined by the BIR, then such Royalty Fees shall be subject to EWT of two percent (2%) which shall be credited against the income tax due on the taxable income of JFC. However, if the payor of the Royalty Fees is not one of the top withholding agents as determined by the BIR, then such Royalty Fees shall not be subject to EWT of two percent (2%) since the said income is not among those enumerated under RR No. 2-1998, as amended.

This ruling is issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation it shall be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request for confirmation of your opinion that Online Loans Pilipinas Financing, Inc. [1] ("OLP") is exempt from payment of withholding tax for services rendered abroad by Tyrads Pte. Ltd., a non-resident foreign corporation ("NRFC").

It is represented that OLP is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the Republic of the Philippines offering financial services such as loans which services are provided through web and mobile applications. TAIaHE

On the other hand, Tyrads Pte. Ltd. is a NRFC registered under the laws of Singapore; that it is not registered as a corporation, partnership or one-person corporation in the Philippines per Certificate of Non-Registration of Company issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission on March 4, 2022; and that it is engaged in the business of advertising services.

On June 6, 2020, the above-mentioned Corporations entered into a Lead Generation Agreement wherein Tyrads Pte. Ltd. shall render advertising services for a fee or renumeration to OLP and said service is rendered in the place of business of the former. Tyrads Pte. Ltd. shall engage Webmasters to place OLP's advertisements on the internet to attract customers. Thereafter, Tyrads Pte. Ltd. shall provide results by providing a statistical data according to the conditions set forth in the placement of the advertisements. OLP will pay Tyrads Pte. Ltd. all incurred charges and fees based on the statistical data provided by the latter.

In this regard, you would like to have confirmation of your opinion that the payment of service fees by OLP to Tyrads Pte. Ltd. is not subject to withholding tax.

In reply, please be informed that Section 23 (F) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, states that a foreign corporation, whether engaged or not in trade or business in the Philippines, is taxable only on income derived from sources within the Philippines. Concerning income from the provision of service, under Section 42 (A) (3) of the Tax Code, as amended, this is considered derived in the Philippines only if the services are actually performed in the Philippines.

The rule in this jurisdiction regarding tax situs is that the source of income is the property, activity or service that produced the income, the test of taxability is the "source" and the source of income is that activity which produced the income. [2] In ascertaining the income source, we must inquire into the property, activity or service that produced the income, or where the inflow of wealth originated. [3] ICHDca

In Aces Philippines Cellular Satellite Corporation vs. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue, [4] the Supreme Court discussed that in determining the income generating activity of NRFC, the services provided in the service agreement must be examined in its entirety or as a whole, and not to single out or compartmentalize one particular activity, thus:

The Court agrees with the CTA that the income-generating activity takes place not during the act of transmission but only upon the gateway's receipt of the call as routed by the satellite. As will be discussed below, the Court identifies the gateway's receipt of the call as the income source as it coincides with (1) the completion or delivery of the service, and (2) the inflow of economic benefits in favor of Aces Bermuda.

1) The gateway's receipt of
the routed call marks the
completion or delivery of the
service.

In rejecting Aces Philippines' attempt to single out the act of transmission as the income producing activity, the Court echoes the CTA En Banc's keen observation that "there is a continuous and very real connection" within the components of the Aces System. While the satellite appears to be the focal point of the system, the Court cannot ignore that there is a two/three-way inter-connection or inter-dependence between/among the satellite in outer space, the control center in Indonesia, and the terminals and gateways in the Philippines.

By itself, the act of transmission only suggests that a Philippine subscriber has made a call and that the satellite received the call and signaled the control center to determine where the call should be routed. At this point, the satellite and its control center have only determined the location the call shall be directed to but have not actually routed the call. Thus, it is clear that nothing has been sold/delivered yet to Aces Philippines. At best, Aces Bermuda's provision of its service remains in-progress at this stage and requires further action to be completed.

That Aces Bermuda's service: (a) relies on the inter-connectivity of the Aces Satellite System's components, and (b) cannot be compartmentalized to the point of transmission are inherent in the nature of its principal undertaking.

The CTA En Banc emphasized that Aces Bermuda undertook to provide satellite communication time to petitioner Aces Philippines. As expressly described in the Air Time Purchase Agreement, Aces Bermuda's provision of satellite communication services relies on the entire Aces System consisting of a satellite that is interconnected with terminals and gateways. The technology was designed precisely to allow local service providers (e.g., Aces Philippines) to access, connect to, and use the Aces Satellite System so that, in turn, the local service providers can cater to their local subscribers (e.g., Philippine subscribers) whose calls require the use of/access to the Aces Satellite System to be able to contact and be connected to another mobile/landline number. cDHAES

Thus, the fulfillment of Aces Bermuda's undertaking requires the satellite to have transmitted/routed the call (first segment) and a gateway to have received the call as routed by the satellite (second segment). At the point of transmission, Aces Philippines has not been given access to the Aces System yet. It is only when the call is actually routed to its gateway that Aces Philippines is able to connect its local subscriber to the intended recipient of the call. In this sense, the gateway's receipt of the call signifies completion/delivery of Aces Bermuda's service.

2) The accrual of satellite air
time fees marks the inflow of
economic benefits.

A reading of Section 3.2 of the Air Time Purchase Agreement, supra, reveals that Aces Bermuda charges satellite air time fees to Aces Philippines according to the latter's usage. Its usage is determined by allocation (Billable Units) based on all calls made to or from Aces Philippines' subscribers utilizing the Aces System — routed through the satellite — regardless of the location of the subscriber at the time of the call or the gateway handling the call. Certainly, Aces Philippines will not be charged anything at the point of transmission inasmuch as there has not been any usage at that time and satellite air time fees expressly exclude satellite utilization time for call set-up, unanswered calls and incomplete calls.

In other words, the satellite air time fees accrue only when the satellite air time is delivered to Aces Philippines (i.e., upon the gateway's receipt of the routed call) and is utilized by the Philippine subscriber for a voice or data call. The accrual of fees payable to Aces Bermuda signifies the inflow of economic benefits. (Citations omitted; Underscoring ours)

In this case, the Lead Generation Agreement expressly states that OLP will pay Tyrads Pte. Ltd. all incurred charges and fees based on the statistical data. 'Statistical data' refers to a detailed report on the customer's lead performance, specifying information on the amount of provided services. The term 'lead' on the other hand, refers to a measurable result (e.g., a purchase, an order, download, etc.) of display of the ads that is achieved by a user completing the necessary action on the customer's website. Based on the said definition, it can be inferred that the statistical data will contain information on how many users availed the services of OLP due to the advertisements provided in different websites. Thus, the provision of the statistical data by Tyrads Pte. Ltd. signifies the inflow of economic benefits which is its income-generating activity. TCAScE

After having identified the source of income, we now inquire into its situs. It is settled that where the inflow of wealth and/or economic benefits proceeds from, and occurs within Philippine territory, it enjoys protection of the Philippine government. In consideration of such protection, the flow of wealth should share the burden of supporting the government, and thus, is subject to tax. [5]

In the Aces Case, the Supreme Court explained how to determine the situs of services performed by a NRFC, to wit:

"1) The income-generating activity is directly associated with the gateways located within Philippine territory.

Verily, Aces Philippines admits that the gateway's receipt of the call as routed by the satellite (i.e., second segment of Aces System) takes place in the Philippines. However, it insists that any income arising therefrom cannot be attributable to Aces Bermuda because: (a) Aces Bermuda's operations are confined to its satellite in outer space; and (b) Aces Philippines, not Aces Bermuda, owns the gateways and related equipment installed in the Philippines.

These contentions do not persuade.

First, the Court has already discussed above that Aces Bermuda's service encompasses both first and second segments of the Aces System's operations. The performance of the service does not cease at the point of transmission but continues until such time Aces Bermuda delivers the satellite communication time (i.e., routes the call) to the Philippine gateway.

Second, while Aces Philippines is the legal owner/operator of the Philippine gateways, it cannot be denied that these gateways were constructed primarily to serve the needs and requirements of the Aces System.

To recall, under the Gateway Agreement executed between PLDT and Aces Indonesia in 1995, Aces Indonesia had supplied PLDT with the necessary equipment and software to enable the latter "to construct, own and operate a [g]ateway or [g]ateways in the Philippines. The construction of the gateways was an act preparatory to the Air Time Purchase Agreement executed in 1997. It was instrumental in and necessary to providing and installing the required technology in the Philippines precisely to join PLDT/Aces Philippines to the Aces Satellite System.

The agreements, taken together, were instrumental in allowing Aces Bermuda to make its services available to Philippine subscribers. The nature of its undertaking necessitates Aces Bermuda to contract service providers in specific jurisdictions like the Philippines. Even if Aces Bermuda operates the satellite in outer space, it cannot provide its services completely even if a territory is within its coverage. It needs: (a) to cause the construction of terrestrial gateways that will receive signals from its satellite; (b) to provide the specific equipment and software to ensure that the gateways are compatible with the Aces System; and (c) to contract a local supplier (e.g., PLDT/Aces Philippines) that would operate the gateways and act as its local distributor of services.

xxx xxx xxx

To stress, the income-generating activity (i.e., accrual of satellite airtime fee payments and completion of the principal undertaking) coincides with the receipt of the routed call by gateways located within Philippine territory. That income generation is dependent on the operations of facilities situated in the Philippines contributes to the income's Philippine situs. Verily, the gateways are legally owned by Aces Philippines. Nonetheless, Aces Bermuda has sufficient economic/beneficial interest in these Philippine properties, inasmuch as its Philippine operations are dependent on these local facilities." (Underscoring supplied)

As previously mentioned, the Lead Generation Agreement states that income payments to Tyrads Pte. Ltd. shall be based on the statistical data. It is the understanding of this Office that the statistical data can only be generated once customers or users from the internet avail the services of OLP because of the advertisements provided by Tyrads Pte. Ltd. Depending on the number of customers or users thereof, it will determine the amount payable to Tyrads Pte. Ltd. Upon careful reading of the Lead Generation Agreement, the posting of the advertisements online and availment of the services advertised allowed Tyrads Pte. Ltd. to perform its services within the Philippine territory. ASEcHI

Based on the foregoing discussions, since the services are considered performed within the Philippines, income payments to Tyrads Pte. Ltd. shall be subject to income tax and, consequently, to withholding tax.

With respect to value-added tax (VAT), Section 108 (A) of the Tax Code, as amended, provides that payments for the sale or exchange of services, including the use or lease of properties are subject to the twelve percent (12%) VAT only if the services are performed in the Philippines. The phrase 'sale or exchange of services' means the performance of all kinds of services in the Philippines for others for a fee, remuneration or consideration Thus, considering the above discussions, income payments made by OLP for the services performed by Tyrads Pte. Ltd. shall be subject to VAT.

Settled is the rule that exemptions from tax are strictly construed against the taxpayer and liberally construed in favor of the taxing authority. One who claims tax exemption must point to a specific provision of law conferring, in clear and plain terms, exemption from the common burden and prove, through substantial evidence, that it is, in fact, covered by the exemption so claimed. [6]

In connection therewith, the rule is that the taxpayer bears the burden of proving that the "income was from sources outside the Philippines and exempt from the application of our income tax law." [7] In light of this context, it is the opinion of this Office that OLP failed to prove that the income payments to Tyrads Pte. Ltd. was solely from sources outside the Philippines. cTDaEH

This ruling is issued on the basis of the facts as represented. However, if upon investigation it shall be disclosed that the actual facts are different, then this ruling shall be without force and effect insofar as the herein parties are concerned.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request for a confirmatory ruling that Pagkakaisa ng mga Naninirahan sa Bangkulasi Homeowners' Association, Inc. (Bangkulasi HOA) is entitled to tax exemption as a non-stock, non-profit corporation under Section 30 of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended.

It is represented that Bangkulasi HOA is a non-stock and non-profit residential homeowners' association duly organized under Section 2 (a) of Executive Order (EO) No. 535 and Section 26 of Republic Act (RA) No. 8763. ITAaHc

In reply, please be informed that Bangkulasi HOA, a residential homeowners association, is not among those non-stock, non-profit corporations contemplated under Section 30 of the Tax Code, as amended, thus, Bangkulasi HOA may not avail of the income tax exemption under the aforesaid provision.

Nevertheless, Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 9-2013 [1] discussed the income taxability of association dues, membership fees, and other assessments/charges collected by a homeowners' association from its homeowner-members and other entities, to wit:

"I. Income Tax — Section 18 of R.A. No. 9904 which exempts from taxation the association dues and income derived from rental subject to certain conditions is an implied recognition by Congress that such receipts are subject to tax under existing laws. Thus, the amounts paid in as dues or fees by homeowner-members of a homeowners' association form part of the gross income of the latter subject to income tax. This is because a homeowners' association furnishes its members with benefits, advantages and privileges in return to such payments. For tax purposes, the association dues, membership fees, and other assessment/charges collected by a homeowners' association constitute income payments or compensation for beneficial services it provides to its member and tenants. The previous interpretation that the assessment dues are funds which are merely held in trust by a homeowners' association lacks legal basis and is hereby abandoned.

Moreover, since a homeowner's association is subject to income tax, income payment made to it are subject to applicable withholding taxes under existing regulations."

In the same vein, RMC No. 9-2013 provides that the association dues and income derived from rentals of Bangkulasi HOA properties may be exempted from income tax provided that the following conditions are complied with pursuant to Section 18 of RA No. 9904:

"a. The homeowners' association must be a duly constituted 'Association' as defined under Section 3 (b) of RA No. 9904;

b. The local government unit having jurisdiction over the homeowners' association must issue certification identifying the basic services being rendered by the homeowners' association and therein stating its lack of resources to render such services notwithstanding its clear mandate under applicable laws, rules and regulations. Provided further, that such services must fall within the purview of the 'basic community services and facilities' which is defined under Section 3 (d) of RA No. 9904 as those referring to service and facilities that redound to the benefit of all homeowners' and from which, by reason of practicality, no homeowner may be excluded such as but not limited to: security; street and vicinity lights' maintenance, repairs and cleaning of streets; garbage collection and disposal; and other similar services and facilities; and

c. The homeowners' association must present proof (i.e., financial statements) that the income and dues are used for the cleanliness, safety, security, and other basic services needed by the members, including the maintenance of the facilities of their respective subdivisions or villages."

In this case, there was no showing that the Bangkulasi HOA met the above conditions for the entitlement of tax exemption under RA No. 9904. In view of the foregoing, your request for the issuance of a Certificate of Tax Exemption pursuant to the Tax Code, as amended, is hereby denied. cSaATC

Please be guided accordingly.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request for confirmation of your opinion that Online Loans Pilipinas Financing, Inc. [1] ("OLP") is exempt from the payment of withholding tax on payments for services rendered abroad by Da Vinci Consult LLC, a non-resident foreign corporation ("NRFC"). CHTAIc

It is represented that OLP is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the Republic of the Philippines offering financial services such as loans which services are provided through web and mobile applications.

On the other hand, Da Vinci Consult LLC is a NRFC registered under the laws of the Russian Federation engaged in the business of risk engine development. It is not registered as a corporation, partnership or one-person corporation in the Philippines per Certificate of Non-Registration of Company issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission on March 24, 2022.

The above-mentioned Corporations entered into two (2) Service Agreements wherein Da Vinci Consult LLC undertakes the performance of the following services for a renumeration which were performed in Da Vinci Consult LLC's head office in Moscow, Russia:

1. Under Service Agreement No. 20210301 dated March 1, 2021, valid until December 1, 2021, Da Vinci Consult LLC shall perform "works on develop risk engine"; and

2. Under Service Agreement No. 082021-1 dated August 31, 2021, valid until December 1, 2021, Da Vinci Consult LLC shall perform "development and IT Technical support work."

In this regard, you would like to have confirmation of your opinion that the payment of service fees by OLP to Da Vinci Consult LLC is not subject to withholding tax.

In reply, please be informed that Section 23 (F) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, states that a foreign corporation, whether engaged or not in trade or business in the Philippines, is taxable only on income derived from sources within the Philippines. Concerning income from the provision of service, under Section 42 (A) (3) of the Tax Code, as amended, this is considered derived in the Philippines only if the services are actually performed in the Philippines. cHDAIS

The rule in this jurisdiction regarding tax situs is that the source of income is the property, activity or service that produced the income, the test of taxability is the "source" and the source of income is that activity which produced the income. [2] With regard to compensation for labor or personal services, services performed within the Philippines, regardless of the residence of the payor, or of the place in which the contract for services was made, or of the place of payment, shall be considered as part of the gross income from sources within the Philippines. Stated differently, the situs of the income derived from labor or personal services is determined solely by the place where service is rendered. [3]

Accordingly, since Da Vinci Consult LLC, a NRFC, performed the services required of it under the agreement outside the Philippines, service fees paid by OLP shall be exempt from income tax pursuant to the above-mentioned provisions.

With respect to value-added tax (VAT), Section 108 (A) of the Tax Code, as amended, provides that payments for the sale or exchange of services, including the use or lease of properties are subject to the twelve percent (12%) VAT only if the services are performed in the Philippines. The phrase 'sale or exchange of services' means the performance of all kinds of services in the Philippines for others for a fee, remuneration or consideration.

Considering that the services by Da Vinci Consult LLC were performed outside the Philippines, the service fees paid therefor by OLP are likewise exempt from VAT.

In view of the foregoing exemptions from income tax and VAT, the payment of service fees by OLP to Da Vinci Consult LLC are not subject to withholding tax.

This ruling is issued on the basis of the facts as represented. However, if upon investigation it shall be disclosed that the actual facts are different, then this ruling shall be without force and effect insofar as the herein parties are concerned. EATCcI

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request for confirmation that the income payments of Online Loans Pilipinas Financing, Inc. ("OLP") to Seon Technologies Kft. ("STK"), is not subject to withholding tax. ISHCcT

Background

1. OLP is a financing company duly organized and existing under the laws of the Philippines engaged in the business of extending credit facilities by way of loan subsidies. The financial services by OLP are offered online via web and mobile applications.

2. STK is a nonresident foreign corporation organized and existing under the laws of Hungary. It is engaged in the business of providing technical support services. STK has no presence in the Philippines as evidenced by the Certificate of Non-registration issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC").

3. OLP and STK entered into a SaaS Services Agreement ("Agreement") where STK will provide a cloud-based machine learning platform ("the "Platform") that allows inputs for user profiling decisions on transaction level in real-time. The Platform will provide a comprehensive information about an online platform user using specific algorithms and information provided by OLP and STK. OLP will be given access to this service by connecting to a set of application programming interfaces ("API") or through graphical user interface provided by STK. The fees for the services of STK include charges for all email API, phone API, IP API, or Device Fingerprint request or call usage. Cost of services comprises all expenses of STK for the fulfillment of the obligations assumed under the Agreement. The fees shall be paid by OLP to STK by transferring funds to STK operating account within thirty (30) days payment term from the issued invoice.

4. STK will perform all the services in its office in Budapest, Hungary.

In reply, please be informed that Section 23 (F) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended ("Tax Code") provides that a "foreign corporation, whether engaged or not in trade or business in the Philippines, is taxable only on income derived from sources within the Philippines." In addition, Section 28 (B) (1) of the Tax Code provides that only income received by a foreign corporation not engaged in trade or business in the Philippines from all sources within the Philippines shall be subject to income tax of twenty five percent (25%). [1]

The rule regarding tax situs is that the source of income is the property, activity or service that produced the income; the test of taxability is the "source" and the source of income is that activity which produced the income. [2] DHITCc

Section 42 (A) (4) of the Tax Code provides that royalties received by non-resident foreign corporation are considered sources within the Philippines, to wit:

"SEC. 42. Income from Sources Within the Philippines. —

(A) Gross Income From Sources Within the Philippines. — The following items of gross income shall be treated as gross income from sources within the Philippines:

xxx xxx xxx

(4) Rentals and Royalties. — Rentals and royalties from property located in the Philippines or from any interest in such property, including rentals or royalties for —

(a) The use of or the right or privilege to use in the Philippines any copyright, patent, design or model, plan, secret formula or process, goodwill, trademark, trade band or other like property or right;

(b) The use of, or the right to use in the Philippines any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment;

(c) The supply of scientific, technical, industrial or commercial knowledge or information; x x x" (Underscoring supplied)

In this case, STK will provide OLP an access to its Platform which will allow OLP to input its customers' and/or potential customers' details for user profiling and/or fraud detection. The Platform will provide a comprehensive information about an online platform user using the information provided by OLP. The information can be acquired by OLP through the provision of its customers' or potential customers' email address, phone number, IP address and digital finger prints.

Based on the foregoing, while it is true that STK is classified for purposes of Philippine taxation as a non-resident foreign corporation, and considering further that all its equipment and system are all located outside the Philippines, a perusal of the agreement between STK and OLP shows that STK is providing OLP a right or privilege to use its Platform for OLP's profiling decisions for the purpose of, among others, verifying whether its customers or potential customers are fraudulent or not. Stated differently, STK is supplying commercial information to OLP through the Platform. It appears that the Platform is a database of online platform users which has the capacity of collating all their information. CAacTH

Such being the case, this Office hereby rules that the income received by STK from the fees OLP is paying for the right to access the Platform is within the purview of "royalty" that is subject to Philippine income tax.

Consequently, said income is subject to final withholding tax pursuant to Section 2.57.1 (F) of Revenue Regulations No. 2-98, [3] as amended, which provides that income derived by a non-resident foreign corporation from all sources within the Philippines are subject to final withholding tax. [4] Hence, OLP is required to withhold a final income tax on the income payments under the aforementioned Agreement.

This ruling is issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation it shall be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue
