Gentlemen :

This refers to your letter requesting on behalf of Fine Properties, Inc. (FPI) for confirmation of your opinion that the basis for the computation of the creditable withholding tax (CWT) and documentary stamp tax (DST) on its transaction involving the sale of real property on installment, should be determined pursuant to the guidelines set under Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 17-2003. [1]

It is represented that on March 26, 2021, FPI and Prime Asset Ventures, Inc. (PAVI) entered into a Contract of Lease over the 123,000 sq.m. portion of Lot 1107 covered by Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) No. 038-2012001481, situated in Brgy. Daan Pare, Orion, Bataan (subject portion). It is stipulated therein that the "rental commencement date" shall be on June 1, 2022 or the commercial operations date of the proposed establishment of "20 MW Bataan Solar Farm Project." The said stipulation is intended to ensure that PAVI will first secure all the pertinent government approvals, clearances and permits necessary for the said project.

On June 24, 2021, by mutual agreement, the parties rescinded the Contract of Lease. Instead, they entered into an Agreement to Purchase and Sale (subject agreement) for the sale of the subject portion which is classified as agricultural lot per Tax Declaration No. 07936 with a gross area of 151,458 sq.m. covered by TCT No. 038-2012001481 (subject property). HEITAD

Under the terms of the subject agreement, the purchase price of the subject portion in the amount of P49,200,000.00 shall be paid by PAVI in installments detailed as follows:

The down payment of P7,200,000.00 is payable as follows:

a. P3,000,000.00 — on June 24, 2021 simultaneous with the execution of the subject agreement as evidenced by Official Receipt No. 5507 issued on the same date.

b. P4,200,000.00 — on or before August 31, 2021 provided FPI has transferred to PAVI the physical and vacant possession of the subject portion.

The remaining P42,000,000.00 shall be paid to FPI on August 31, 2023 or upon release of the title and tax declaration covering the subject portion registered in its name, whichever comes earlier.

The subject agreement likewise provides that FPI shall execute the Deed of Sale upon the full payment by PAVI of the purchase price. Simultaneously, FPI shall deliver to PAVI the original owner's duplicate copy of the title to the subject portion free from any lien, encumbrance and annotation, the tax declaration and such other related documents or the original owner's duplicate of the title covering the subject property.

Emphatically, the prevailing zonal value of covering the subject portion is P25.00 per square meter as of the time of the execution of the subject agreement.

On July 12, 2021, PAVI through its authorized representative filed an application for reclassification of the subject property from agricultural land to industrial use before the Sangguniang Bayan of Orion, Bataan. On August 20, 2021, the Sangguniang Bayan enacted Municipal Special Ordinance No. 21-040-194 (special ordinance) approving the reclassification of the subject property. The special ordinance was duly ratified by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of the Province of Bataan on September 13, 2021 pursuant to Resolution No. 356, and was duly approved by Governor Albert S. Garcia on October 1, 2021. Accordingly, Tax Declaration No. 21888 was issued on December 28, 2021 reflecting the reclassification of the subject property to industrial.

Meanwhile, on August 31, 2021, PAVI paid the second installment to FPI. On even date, the latter issued Official Receipt No. 5545 exhibiting the second installment.

From the foregoing, your request for a ruling confirming that the subject agreement is a sale of real property on installment and the basis for the computation of the CWT and DST is the highest value among the zonal, market value per tax declaration at the time of the subject agreement in accordance with Section 3 (J) of RR No. 17-2003. DETACa

In reply, please be informed that Section 3 (J) of RR No. 17-2003 provides for the tax treatment of sale involving real properties classified as ordinary asset:

"Sec. 2.57.2. Income Payment Subject to Creditable Withholding Tax and Rates Prescribed Thereon. — Except as herein otherwise provided, there shall be withheld a creditable income tax at the rates herein specified for each class of payee from the following items of income payments to persons residing in the Philippines:

xxx xxx xxx

(J) Gross selling price or total amount of consideration or its equivalent paid to the seller/owner for the sale, exchange, or transfer of real property classified as ordinary asset. — x x x

xxx xxx xxx

However, if the buyer is engaged in trade or business, whether a corporation or otherwise, these rules shall apply:

(i) If the sale is a sale of property on the installment plan [i.e., payments in the year of sale do not exceed twenty five percent (25%) of the selling price], the tax shall be deducted and withheld by the buyer from every installment which tax shall be based on the ratio of actual collection of the consideration against the agreed consideration appearing in the Contract to Sell applied to the gross selling price or fair market value of the property at the time of the execution of the Contract to Sell, whichever is higher.

xxx xxx xxx

For sale of property on installment basis or deferred payment basis where the Contract to Sell is always executed before the execution of the Deed of Sale, the said Contract to Sell must be attached to the Deed of Absolute Sale executed upon completion of the payments and the duly notarized original duplicate copy of both documents must be presented to the RDO having jurisdiction of the place where the property is located for validation of the correctness of issuance of CAR/TCL. aScITE

It is to be noted, however, that in case of sale of real property paid under installment payment or deferred payment basis, the payment of the documentary stamp tax (DST) shall accrue upon the execution of the Deed of Absolute Sale but the basis for the imposition thereof shall be the gross selling price or fair market value of the property, whichever is higher, at the time of the execution of the Contract to Sell." (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

The provision clearly states the tax consequence of DST which accrues upon the execution of the deed of absolute sale is reckoned from the gross selling price or fair market value of the property at the time of the execution of the contract to sell.

Insofar as CWT, Section 3 (J) of RR No. 17-2003 provides that if the sale of a real property is on installment plan, the tax shall be deducted and withheld by the buyer from every installment which tax shall be based on the ratio of actual collection of the consideration against the agreed consideration appearing in the contract to sell applied to the gross selling price or fair market value of the property at the time of the execution of the contract to sell, whichever is higher. The same provision likewise mandates the contract to sell to be attached with the deed of absolute sale executed upon completion of the payments and the duly notarized original duplicate copy of both documents must be presented to the Revenue District Office (RDO) having jurisdiction of the place where the property is located for validation of the correctness of the issuance of an electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR).

These provisos readily suggest that the CWT is made to be predicated upon the object and the consideration agreed upon by the parties as contained in the contract to sell and the deed of sale. This conclusion stems from Article 1475 of the New Civil Code which provides that:

"Article 1475. The contract of sale is perfected at the moment there is a meeting of minds upon the thing which is the object of the contract and upon the price.

From that moment, the parties may reciprocally demand performance, subject to the provisions of the law governing the form of contracts."

As tax laws are civil in nature, [2] it is worthy to note the stages of a contract of sale, which are (1) negotiation, covering the period from the time the prospective contracting parties indicate interest in the contract to the time the contract is perfected; (2) perfection, which takes place upon the concurrence of the essential elements of the sale, which is the meeting of the minds of the parties as to the object of the contract and upon the price; and (3) consummation, which begins when the parties perform their respective undertakings under the contract of sale, culminating in the extinguishment thereof. [3]

The contract to sell coupled with the deed of absolute sale indicates the acquiescence to and acknowledgment of the parties towards the validity of the sale. Considered collectively, both contract to sell and deed of sale present the time line when the parties have perfected their contract and their intention as shown by the terminology used including all the surrounding circumstances, such as their relative situation at that time, their attitude, acts, conduct, declarations, their negotiations leading to the deed, and generally, all pertinent facts tending to fix and determine the real nature of their design and their corresponding obligations. CAIHTE

The inclusion of the notarized deed of absolute sale to be presented before the RDO signifies that in computing for the CWT, the legal consequences of the conveyance produce only its effects, insofar as the Bureau of Internal Revenue is concerned, after the notarization of the said document. This can be gleaned from the rule that a private conveyance is valid between the parties [4] and does not include those who are not privy thereto. The necessity of a public document for contracts which transmit or extinguish real rights over immovable property, as mandated by Article 1358 of the New Civil Code, is only for convenience [5] or to bind third persons. [6] This is in line with the implications under the rules of evidence as elaborated in the case Dela Rama v. Papa, [7] viz.:

"Under Section 19, Rule 132 of the Rules of Court, documents acknowledged before a notary public except for last wills and testaments are deemed as public documents, and as such, under Section 23 of the same Rule, they are evidence of the fact which gave rise to its execution and as to its date." (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

The attachment of the notarized contract to sell, in addition to the said deed of sale, manifests that the legal consequences of the conveyance retroacts from the time the contract of sale is perfected. It is during this time that the presumed gain or profit is realized or received, actually or constructively. Logically, the prevailing conditions during such time of perfection shall be the basis determining the tax liabilities of the parties.

From the foregoing, this Office hereby confirms your opinion that the computation of CWT and DST should be based on the gross selling price or fair market value of the subject portion, whichever is higher, at the time of the execution of the subject agreement pursuant to the Section 3 (J) of RR No. 17-2003.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be ascertained that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void. HTcADC

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Attention: Alejandro H. Tengco

Chairman and Chief Executive Officer

Gentlemen :

This refers to your letter, on behalf of the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation ("PAGCOR"), requesting for a ruling that PAGCOR's purchase of slot machines from its non-resident foreign corporation not engaged in trade or business supplier (the "Non-resident Supplier") is exempt from taxes and/or subject to value-added tax ("VAT") at zero percent (0%) rate regardless of Section 7 of Republic Act ("RA") No. 11534, which states that a nonresident foreign corporation shall pay a tax equal to twenty five percent (25%) of the gross income received during each taxable year. HTcADC

As represented, PAGCOR is to purchase slot machines pursuant to its authority to operate games of chance in the Philippines. Among the suppliers of PAGCOR is the Non-resident Supplier. Considering that the tax exemption granted to PAGCOR by virtue of Presidential Decree ("PD") No. 1869 extends to all juridical entities with a contractual relationship with PAGCOR without any qualification, it is the position of PAGCOR that the same extends to its non-resident foreign corporation not engaged in trade or business suppliers.

In reply, please be informed that Section 13 of PD No. 1869, as amended, reads:

"SECTION 13. Exemptions. —

xxx xxx xxx

(2) Income and Other Taxes. — (a) Franchise Holder: No tax of any kind or form, income or otherwise, as well as fees, charges or levies of whatever nature, whether National or Local, shall be assessed and collected under this Franchise from the Corporation; nor shall any form of tax or charge attach in any way to the earnings of the Corporation, except a Franchise Tax of five (5%) percent of the gross revenue or earnings derived by the Corporation from its operation under this Franchise. Such tax shall be due and payable quarterly to the National Government and shall be in lieu of all kinds of taxes, levies, fees or assessments of any kind, nature or description, levied, established or collected by any municipal, provincial, or national government authority.

(b) Others: The exemption herein granted for earnings derived from the operations conducted under the franchise specifically from the payment of any tax, income or otherwise, as well as any form of charges, fees or levies, shall inure to the benefit of and extend to corporation(s), association(s), agency(ies), or individual(s) with whom the Corporation or operator has any contractual relationship in connection with the operations of the casino(s) authorized to be conducted under this Franchise and to those receiving compensation or other remuneration from the Corporation or operator as a result of essential facilities furnished and/or technical services rendered to the Corporation or operator. CAIHTE

The fee or remuneration of foreign entertainers contracted by the Corporation or operator in pursuance of this provision shall be free of any tax." (Underscoring supplied)

Based on the above provision, a franchise tax of five (5%) percent shall be imposed on PAGCOR based on its gross revenue or earnings from gaming operations under its franchise in lieu of all kinds of taxes (whether direct or indirect), levies, fees or assessments of any kind, nature or description, levied, established or collected by any municipal, provincial, or national government authority. This tax incentive also extends to: (1) corporations, associations, agencies or individuals with whom PAGCOR or operator has any contractual relationship in connection with the operations of authorized casino(s); and (2) to those receiving compensation or other remuneration from PAGCOR or operator as a result of essential facilities furnished and/or technical services rendered to the PAGCOR or operator.

The above tax exemption includes VAT pursuant to Section 109 (1) (K) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended ("Tax Code") which states that:

"SEC 109. Exempt Transactions. — (1) Subject to the provisions of Subsection (2) hereof, the following transactions shall be exempt from the value-added tax:

xxx xxx xxx

(K) Transactions which are exempt under international agreements to which the Philippines is a signatory or under special laws, except those under Presidential Decree No. 529." (underlining supplied)

Please note that in granting the above tax incentives, Section 13 of PD No. 1869, as amended, does not distinguish the residency of PAGCOR's contractees. It is a well-settled rule that where the law does not distinguish, neither should we distinguish. [1] Also, a cardinal rule in statutory construction is that when the law is clear and free from any doubt or ambiguity, there is no room for construction or interpretation. There is only room for application. [2] As the statute is clear, plain, and free from ambiguity, it must be given its literal meaning and applied without attempted interpretation. This is what is known as the plain-meaning rule or verba legis. Furthermore, there is the maxim verba legis non est recedendum, or "from the words of a statute there should be no departure." Therefore, it may be concluded that it applies to both domestic and foreign corporation, whether resident or non-resident.

In line with the above legal principle, the BIR, in several rulings, did not qualify the residency of the contractees of PACCOR. [3] In BIR Ruling No. 382-2019, [4] the BIR stated that "[S]ince PGI is a registered supplier and contractor of PAGCOR for the Gaming Products and Services, as above-mentioned, and thus, having a contractual relationship with the latter, the exemption from taxes, fees and charges enjoyed by PAGCOR is extended to PGI pursuant to Section 13 (2) (b) of PD 1869, as amended." In issuing the said ruling, the major consideration made by the BIR is whether the entity is a contractor of PAGCOR for the latter's gaming operations, which is, to emphasize, the only qualification mandated under Section 13 (b) of PD No. 1869, as amended. aScITE

In the recent en banc decision of the Supreme Court in the consolidated cases of Saint Wealth Ltd. v. Bureau of Internal Revenue and Marco Polo Enterprises Limited v. Secretary of Finance, [5] citing also the case of Bloomberry Resorts and Hotels, Inc. v. Bureau of Internal Revenue, [6] the Supreme Court unequivocally affirmed the applicability of the tax exemption provisions of PD No. 1869, as amended, to PAGCOR's contractees and licensees without any qualification, to wit:

"Considering the above-cited provisions, this Court clarified in Bloomberry Resorts and Hotels, Inc. v. Bureau of Internal Revenue (Bloomberry), that PAGCOR's tax privilege of paying only a five percent (5%) franchise tax for income generated from its gaming operations, in lieu of all other taxes, inures to the benefit of PAGCOR's licensees:

'As the PAGCOR Charter states in unequivocal terms that exemptions granted for earnings derived from the operations conducted under the franchise specifically from the payment of any tax, income or otherwise, as well as any form of charges, fees or levies, shall inure to the benefit of and extend to corporation(s), association(s), agency(ies), or individual(s) with whom the PAGCOR or operator has any contractual relationship in connection with the operations of the casino(s) authorized to be conducted under this Franchise, so it must be that all contractees and licensees of PAGCOR, upon payment of the 5% franchise tax, shall likewise be exempted from all other taxes, including corporate income tax realized from the operation of casinos.

xxx xxx xxx

Plainly, too, upon payment of the 5% franchise tax, petitioner's income from its gaming operations of gambling casinos, gaming clubs and other similar recreation or amusement places, and gaming pools, defined within the purview of the aforesaid section, is not subject to corporate income tax.'" (Underscoring supplied)

The rationale for the applicability of the tax exemption provisions of PD No. 1869 to PAGCOR's contractees and licensees was explained in the case of CIR v. Acesite (Philippines) Hotel Corp., [7] viz.: DETACa

"Indeed, by extending the exemption to entities or individuals dealing with PAGCOR, the legislature clearly granted exemption also from indirect taxes. It must be noted that the indirect tax of VAT, as in the instant case, can be shifted or passed to the buyer, transferee, or lessee of the goods, properties, or services subject to VAT. Thus, by extending the tax exemption to entities or individuals dealing with PAGCOR in casino operations, it is exempting PAGCOR from being liable to indirect taxes."

In light of the recent rulings and jurisprudence, it is clear that income received by: (1) PAGCOR; and (2) PAGCOR's contractees and licensees (whether domestic or resident/nonresident foreign corporation), from their respective gaming operations, is subject to five percent (5%) franchise tax, in lieu of all other national and local taxes, including indirect taxes such as VAT.

In the instant case, a perusal of the documents submitted shows that the slot machines that will be sold by the Non-resident Supplier to PAGCOR will be used by the latter in its gaming operations. Hence, income derived by said Non-resident Supplier from the sale is considered as income by a contractee of PAGCOR derived from gaming operations, which falls squarely under Section 13 (b) of PD No. 1869, as amended.

Such being the case, this Office hereby rules that the income derived by Non-resident supplier (being a contractee of PAGCOR) from the sale of slot machines to PAGCOR is subject to five percent (5%) franchise tax, in lieu of all other national and local taxes, including the twenty-five percent (25%) income tax based on Section 7 of RA No. 11534 and indirect taxes such as VAT.

Relative thereto, the gross income derived from all sources within the Philippines by a non-resident foreign corporation is subject to final withholding tax pursuant to Section 2.57.1 (F) of Revenue Regulations No. 2-98, as amended. Thus, in this particular situation, PAGCOR shall subject the payments to its non-resident foreign corporation suppliers to the final withholding tax at the rate of five percent (5%) representing the franchise tax, in lieu of all other national and local taxes.

However, it should be noted that income derived by the Non-resident Supplier from other related services/operations or from non-gaming operations in the Philippines, if any, shall be subject to the regular internal revenue taxes, including, but not limited to, corporate income tax and VAT.

This ruling is issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation it shall be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void. HEITAD

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Office of the President of the Philippines
Malacañang Complex
J.P. Laurel Street
San Miguel, Manila, 1005

Attention: Atty. Lynn Danao-Moreno, JD, MPM, CESO II

Assistant Executive Secretary

General Government Administration Office, and Executive Director

Gentlemen :

This refers to your letter on behalf of the Office of the President-Provident Fund Management Office requesting to clarify whether health and maintenance organization ("HMO") services availed of/purchased by the Office of the President-Provident Fund (the "Fund") for the benefit of its members from Maxicare Healthcare Corporation ("Maxicare") is subject to twelve percent (12%) value-added tax ("VAT"). HTcADC

Background

1. The Fund was established by virtue of Memorandum Order ("MO") No. 109, issued by former President Joseph Ejercito Estrada on August 15, 2000, to provide supplementary benefits to member-employees.

2. MO No. 109 was issued pursuant to Section 41 of the General Provisions of Republic Act ("RA") No. 7180, otherwise known as the F.Y. 1992 General Appropriations Act, [1] as implemented by Administrative Order ("AO") No. 279, series of 1992. [2]

3. Section 41 of the General Provisions of RA No. 7180 mandated the establishment of agency Provident Funds to be sourced from service fees collections, and for the Office of the President to promulgate rules and regulations for the same.

4. Consequently, the late President Corazon C. Aquino issued AO No. 279 prescribing the rules and regulations for the establishment and administration of Provident Funds for agencies covered by Section 41 of the General Provisions or RA No. 7180.

5. The initial sources of the Fund are the President's social fund in the amount of PhP5.0 million and the Office of the President Trust Fund in the amount of PhP10.0 million. Also, member-employees shall contribute monthly to the Fund equivalent to three percent (3%) of their monthly basic salary through payroll deduction, and the Office of the President shall provide a counterpart contribution equivalent to six percent (6%) of the member-employees' monthly basic salary, which may vary over the years depending on the availability of funds. The Fund may also accept donations from various sources. CAIHTE

6. Contributions to the Fund are withdrawable only upon retirement, death, separation from service, or permanent physical disability of the member-employees.

7. Pursuant to MO No. 109 and its implementing rules and regulations, the Board of Trustees may provide various benefits to member-employees, and invest the funds. Any income derived by the Fund is being distributed to the member-employees in the form of annual dividends and patronage refund for the loaning facility being availed of by member-employees. Aside from dividends and patronage refund, member-employees also receive other benefits such as anniversary bonus, Christmas tokens, one-time accident insurance, and recently, an HMO purchased from Maxicare.

8. Contrary to the position of Maxicare, the Office of the President-Provident Fund Management Office maintains that the Fund, being in the nature of a retirement fund, is exempt from tax pursuant to Section 32 (B) (6) of the Tax Code, which provides retirement benefits, pensions, gratuities, etc. are excluded from the gross income, and therefore, non-taxable.

In reply, please be informed that Sections 105 and 108 of National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended ("Tax Code"), provide that a twelve percent (12%) VAT shall be levied, assessed and collected based on the gross sales derived by entities rendering services, to wit:

"SEC. 105. Persons Liable. — Any person who, in the course of trade or business, sells, barters, exchanges, leases goods or properties, renders services, and any person who imports goods shall be subject to the value-added tax (VAT) imposed in Sections 106 to 108 of this Code.

xxx xxx xxx

The phrases "in the course of trade or business" means the regular conduct or pursuit of a commercial or an economic activity, including transactions incidental thereto, by any person regardless of whether or not the person engaged therein is a non-stock, non-profit private organization (irrespective of the disposition of its net income and whether or not it sells exclusively to members or their guests), or government entity.

xxx xxx xxx

SEC. 108. Value-Added Tax on Sale of Services and Use or Lease of Properties. —

(A) Rate and Base of Tax. — There shall be levied, assessed and collected, a value-added tax equivalent to twelve percent (12%) of gross receipts derived from the sale or exchange of services, including the use or lease of properties. aScITE

The phrase "sale or exchange of services" means the performance of all kinds of services in the Philippines for others for a fee, remuneration or consideration, including those performed or rendered by construction and service contractors; stock, real estate, commercial, customs and immigration brokers; lessors of property, whether personal or real; warehousing services; lessors or distributors of cinematographic films; persons engaged in milling, processing, manufacturing or repacking goods for others; proprietors, operators or keepers of hotels, motels, rest houses, pension houses, inns, resorts; proprietors or operators of restaurants, refreshment parlors, cafes and other eating places, including clubs and caterers; dealers in securities; lending investors; transportation contractors on their transport of goods or cargoes, including persons who transport goods or cargoes for hire another domestic common carriers by land relative to their transport of goods or cargoes; common carriers by air and sea relative to their transport of passengers, goods or cargoes from one place in the Philippines to another place in the Philippines; sales of electricity by generation companies, transmission by any means entity, and distribution companies, including electric cooperatives; services of franchise grantees of electric utilities, telephone and telegraph, radio and television broadcasting and all other franchise grantees except those under Section 119 of this Code, and non-life insurance companies (except their crop insurances), including surety, fidelity, indemnity, and bonding companies; and similar services regardless of whether or not the performance thereof calls for the exercise or use of the physical or mental faculties.

xxx xxx xxx

For purposes of this section, the term "gross sales" means the total amount of money or its equivalent representing the contract price, compensation, service fee, rental or royalty, including the amount charged for materials supplied with the services and deposits and advanced payments actually or constructively received during the taxable quarter for the services performed or to be performed for another person, which the purchaser pays or is obligated to pay to the seller in consideration of the sale, barter, or exchange of services that has already been rendered by the seller and the use or lease of properties that have already been supplied by the seller, excluding value-added tax and those amounts earmarked for payment to third (3rd) party or received as reimbursement for payment on behalf of another which do not redound to the benefit of the seller as provided under relevant laws, rules or regulations: Provided, That for long-term contracts for a period of one (1) year or more, the invoice shall be issued on the month in which the service, or use or lease of properties is rendered or supplied." (Emphases and underscoring supplied)

Under Revenue Memorandum Circular ("RMC") No. 56-2002, [3] citing Court of Tax Appeals Case No. 6166, entitled "Philippine Health Care Providers, Inc. vs. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue," dated April 05, 2002, the Bureau of Internal Revenue ("BIR") clarified that HMO providers are not actually rendering medical service but merely acting as a conduit between the members and their accredited and recognized hospitals and clinics. What is being taxed are the services rendered by HMO providers in providing and arranging for the provisions of health care services to its respective members in exchange for a pre-negotiated, pre-paid membership fees. Therefore, sale by HMO providers of HMO services to its customers are subject to twelve percent (12%) VAT based on their gross receipts, unless expressly exempted by any law, rules or regulations. [4] DETACa

A perusal of AO No. 279, MO No. 109, the Tax Code and other relevant laws, rules and regulations, shows that no exemption from tax of whatever nature, whether direct or indirect, such as VAT, is granted to the income derived or purchases of goods or services by the provident funds established pursuant to Section 41 of the General Provisions of RA No. 7180. The absence of an express statutory provision exempting the subject transaction from VAT stimulates the inevitable application of Sections 105 and 108 of the Tax Code. Consequently, Maxicare's sale of HMO services to the Fund is subject to twelve percent (12%) VAT.

In establishing tax exemptions, it should be borne in mind that taxation is the rule, exemption is the exception. Accordingly, statutes granting tax exemptions must be construed in strictissimi juris against the taxpayer and liberally in favor of the taxing authority. One who claims an exemption from tax payments rests the burden of justifying the exemption by words too plain to be mistaken and too categorical to be misinterpreted. [5] It cannot be over-emphasized that tax exemption represents a loss of revenue to the government and must, therefore, not rest on vague inference. Exemption from taxation is never presumed. For tax exemption to be recognized the grant must be clear and express; it cannot be made to rest on doubtful implications.

The legal bases raised by the Fund to support the exemption of the sale of HMO service by Maxicare to the Fund from twelve percent (12%) VAT are: (1) the establishment of the Fund was mandated by law, hence, exempt from taxes; and (2) Section 32 (B) (6) of the Tax Code. This Office is of the opinion that the cited legal bases are misplaced based on the following grounds:

First, while it is true that the Fund is established by law, as thoroughly discussed above, there are no provisions in the same granting any tax exemption. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that its purchases are exempt from tax, such as VAT.

Second, income tax and VAT are two separate and distinct internal revenue taxes. Section 32 (B) (6) of the Tax Code is a provision under the chapter for income tax. Hence, unless otherwise stated, income tax provisions (such as Section 32 (B) (6) of the Tax Code) cannot be used in determining whether a particular transaction is subject to VAT.

Lastly, Section 32 (B) (6) of the Tax Code refers to the exclusion of retirement benefits, pensions, gratuities, and other similar benefits received by employees under certain laws (i.e., RA No. 7641, [6] reasonable private benefit plan maintained by the employer, RA No. 8291, [7] or RA No. 8282) [8] from their respective gross income subject to income tax. On the other hand, the subject matter of this request pertains to the purchase of HMO services by the Fund. Clearly, they refer to different transactions. Hence, Section 32 (B) (6) of the Tax Code is not applicable to the subject matter. HEITAD

Having all these in regard, this Office hereby rules that the sale by Maxicare of HMO services to the Fund is subject to twelve percent (12%) VAT.

This ruling is issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation it shall be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Attention: William Benson S. Gan

Tax Services

Gentlemen :

This refers to your letter request on behalf of your client, Easytrip Services Corporation (Company), for a confirmation that the amounts received by the Company from banks and credit card companies, authorized partner merchants, and corporate clients relating to loads and reloads, which are merely held in trust and for remittance to the toll operators, are exempt from expanded withholding tax (EWT).

It is represented that the Company is primarily engaged in the business of providing services related to Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) systems which include, among others, the implementation of inter-operability of the different toll collection systems of tollways in the Philippines, account management and funding management of all electronic pass issued. The Company earns revenue by charging service fees to toll operators based on the Company's ETC performance with respect to electronic toll collection transaction count. On the other hand, the toll passage fees for the use/access of expressways will form part of the income of the respective toll operators, as these pertain to the use of the toll roads. aDSIHc

Particular to its management of electronic passes, the Company observes the process of issuing transponder gadgets/stickers and the maintenance/monitoring of its loads and reloads. The gadget allows users to access tollways and tender payments for use of such facility.

The payments for loads and reloads are available to the tollway users through cash, auto-debit arrangement (ADA) through credit cards, debit card or any other payment means. For ADA and debit cards, the Company will utilize banks and credit card companies.

Other options for tollway users to reload their electronic passes are available through the company-controlled stations and authorized partner merchants. There are also corporate clients where the Company will send them a statement of their actual tollway usage either on a weekly or semi-monthly basis.

It is further represented that the cash received by the Company from public users are considered as liabilities of the Company. This is because the said amount will: 1.) be remitted by the Company to the toll operators upon receipt of the report of actual usage by the user; or 2.) be refunded to the user, should the user expressly intend to not use the gadget and request to be refunded thereof.

The loads and reloads made by users through the banks via ADA through credit cards are subject to the usual bank charges and 0.5% EWT pursuant to Section 2.57.2 (H) of Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 02-98, as amended. ATICcS

Hence, this request.

In reply, please be informed that Section 57 (B) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, provides:

Sec. 57. Withholding of Tax at Source. —

xxx xxx xxx

B) Withholding of Creditable Tax at Source. — The Secretary of Finance may, upon the recommendation of the Commissioner, require the withholding of a tax on the items of income payable to natural or juridical persons, residing in the Philippines, by payor-corporation/persons as provided for by law, at the rate of not less than one percent (1%) but not more than thirty-two percent (32%) thereof, which shall be credited against the income tax liability of the taxpayer for the taxable year.

In connection thereto, Section 2.57 (B) of RR No. 2-98, as amended, provides, as follows:

SECTION 2.57. Withholding of Tax at Source. —

(B) Creditable Withholding Tax. — Under the creditable withholding tax system, taxes withheld on certain income payments are intended to equal or at least approximate the tax due of the payee on said income. The income recipient is still required to file an income tax return, as prescribed in Sec. 51 and Sec. 52 of the NIRC, as amended, to report the income and/or pay the difference between the tax withheld and the tax due on the income. Taxes withheld on income payments covered by the expanded withholding tax (referred to in Sec. 2.57.2 of these regulations) and compensation income (referred to in Sec. 2.78 also of these regulations) are creditable in nature.

Under the withholding tax system, taxes withheld on certain income payments are intended to equal or at least approximate the tax due of the payee on said income. Thus, taxes withheld are in the nature of advance payment by a taxpayer in order to extinguish his possible tax obligation. Taxes withheld are installments on the annual tax which may be due at the end of the taxable year.

The obligation to withhold taxes is premised on the condition that amounts remitted involve income payment from the payor such that the payee received taxable income. ETHIDa

Income, in a broad sense, means all wealth that flows into the taxpayer other than as return of capital. Income, for tax purposes, is the amount of money coming to a person or corporation within a specified time, whether as payment for services, interest, or profits from investment.

The receipt of cash advance will not result in a flow of wealth because the Company shall likewise recognize a liability. Since the advances are not considered as income, it is therefore not subject to income tax or creditable withholding tax, there being no income payment to the extent of the liability recognized. Otherwise stated, when the Company receives the money from toll users through 1) banks; 2) company-controlled stations; and 3) authorized partner merchants, the same shall not automatically constitute as an income because of the recognition or a liability. Consequently, there being no flow of wealth to the Company, the withholding therefore by 1) banks; 2) company-controlled stations; and 3) authorized partner merchant is not warranted.

Nonetheless, the service fees charged embodied on the questioned transactions as well as the other fees and income which redound to the benefit of the Company by holding on to said cash advance, other than mere return of capital, shall be subject to income tax and consequently to creditable withholding tax as the same form part of the Company's income, as represented. The service fees are likewise subject to value-added tax (VAT). Also, payment or amount of loads or reloads that were not used and refunded by the users shall be considered as income of the Company and shall be subject to income tax, withholding tax and VAT.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be ascertained that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request on behalf of M.C. Holdings Corporation for reconsideration of a portion of BIR Ruling No. 1011-2018 dated June 13, 2018, particularly the portion which provides as follows: HEITAD

"Thus, property dividends which constitute stocks in trade or properties primarily held for sale or lease, which shall be distributed by M.C. HOLDINGS CORPORATION to its stockholders and declared out of its retained earnings shall be subject to VAT based on the FMV or zonal valuation whichever is higher, at the time of distribution. (BIR Ruling No. 190-99 dated November 29, 1999)"

In your request for reconsideration, you stated that M.C. Holdings Corporation is a Non-VAT registered entity. Therefore, Section 106 (B) (2) (a) of the National Internal Revenue Code (Tax Code) of 1997, as amended, and Section 4.106-7 (a) (2) of RR No. 16-2005, as amended, are not applicable.

In reply, please be advised that your request for exemption is denied.

Basic is the rule in taxation that a person claiming exemption is burdened to prove his or her claims to tax authorities with sufficient and competent evidence. In the case of National Power Corporation vs. Province of Isabela, [1] the Supreme Court ruled:

"Indeed, taxation is the rule and exemption is the exception. The burden of proof rests upon the party claiming exemption to prove that it is, in fact, covered by the exemption so claimed. Tax exemptions should be granted only by clear and unequivocal provision of law on the basis of language too plain to be mistaken. They cannot be extended by mere implication or inference."

In this instant case, unfortunately, you failed to satisfy this heavy burden. Being subject to VAT does not rest upon a taxpayer's registration. A person, whether VAT-registered or not, may be liable for VAT. It is the Tax Code of 1997, as amended, that determines whether a person is liable for VAT. For instance, a person who earns beyond the VAT threshold becomes liable for VAT even if he is not VAT-registered. Another example would be for imports, where a person is liable for VAT on imports regardless of whether he is VAT-registered or not. aDSIHc

Lastly, please be informed that Revenue Memorandum Order (RMO) No. 9-2014 [2] requires that documentary requirements to be submitted to the Bureau of Internal Revenue should be certified true copies and letter requests seeking tax exemptions should be under oath. In this case, none of the requirements mentioned were satisfied.

All these considered, this Office is constrained from issuing a tax ruling due to noncompliance with the requirements in RMO No. 9-2014 and denies your claim for lack of legal basis. This, however, is without prejudice to the filing of another request for ruling.

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.

Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request on behalf of your client, Air Liquide Philippines, Inc. (Air Liquide) for confirmation of your opinion that the termination fee to be received by Air Liquide from Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corporation (Pilipinas Shell) on account of the termination of the Hydrogen Supply Agreement (Subject Agreement) previously entered into by the parties is subject to income tax and value-added tax (VAT). ATICcS

It is represented that on July 12, 2019, Air Liquide and Pilipinas Shell entered into the Subject Agreement whereby Air Liquide agreed to process Pilipinas Shell's natural gas for a stipulated monthly fee for the next twenty (20) years. The Subject Agreement entailed the construction of a Hydrogen Manufacturing Unit and a Liquid Carbon Dioxide Plant by Air Liquide, customized specifically for Pilipinas Shell on the latter's refinery in Tabangao, Batangas. The construction of the Plants commenced in 2020 and was scheduled to be completed and operational in the first quarter of 2021. In August 2020, the Board of Directors of Pilipinas Shell decided to cease refinery operations and close the Tabangao Refinery. This closure meant that the Subject Agreement entered into by the parties will no longer be needed. On December 23, 2020, Air Liquide and Pilipinas Shell executed another agreement (Termination Agreement) whereby Pilipinas Shell agreed to pay Air Liquide a Termination Fee of the Subject Agreement amounting to Thirty-Six Million, Five Hundred Thousand US Dollars (36,500,000.00USD) by way of On-Shore bank transfer converted from US Dollars to Philippine Peso with the latest reference exchange rate used by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas at the Invoicing Date (January 25, 2021 and January 25, 2022).

In reply, please be informed that Section 105 of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, delineates the imposition of VAT only on sale, barter, exchange, lease, rendering of service or importation of goods, viz.: ETHIDa

"SEC. 105. Persons Liable. — Any person who, in the course of trade or business, sells, barters, exchanges, leases goods or properties, renders services, and any person who imports goods shall be subject to the value-added tax (VAT) imposed in Sections 106 to 108 of this Code.

xxx xxx xxx

The phrase 'in the course of trade or business' means the regular conduct or pursuit of a commercial or an economic activity, including transactions incidental thereto, by any person regardless of whether or not the person engaged therein is a non-stock, nonprofit private organization (irrespective of the disposition of its net income and whether or not it sells exclusively to members or their guests), or government entity." (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

In consonance thereto, Sections 4.105-1 and 4.105-2 of Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 16-2005, as amended, states that:

"SECTION 4.105-1. Persons Liable. — Any person who, in the course of his trade or business, sells, barters, exchanges or leases goods or properties, or renders services, and any person who imports goods, shall be liable to VAT imposed in Secs. 106 to 108 of the Tax Code.

xxx xxx xxx

'Person' refers to any individual, trust, estate, partnership, corporation, joint venture, cooperative or association.

'Taxable person' refers to any person liable for the payment of VAT, whether registered or registrable in accordance with Sec. 236 of the Tax Code.

xxx xxx xxx

"Taxable sale" refers to the sale, barter, exchange and/or lease of goods or properties, including transactions "deemed sale" and the performance of service for a consideration, whether in cash or in kind, all of which are subject to tax under Secs. 106 and 108 of the Tax Code.

SECTION 4.105-2. Nature and Characteristics of VAT. — VAT is a tax on consumption levied on the sale, barter, exchange or lease of goods or properties and services in the Philippines and on importation of goods into the Philippines. The seller is the one statutorily liable for the payment of the tax but the amount of the tax may be shifted or passed on to the buyer, transferee or lessee of the goods, properties or services. This rule shall likewise apply to existing contracts of sale or lease of goods, properties or services at the time of the effectivity of RA No. 9337. However, in the case of importation, the importer is the one liable for the VAT." (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

The above-quoted provisions are clear that VAT is levied to any individual, trust, estate, partnership, corporation, joint venture, cooperative or association on their sale, barter, exchange or lease of goods or properties and services in the Philippines and on the importation of goods into the Philippines. TIADCc

The proceeds of the Termination Agreement in favor of Air Liquide, represents not only the indemnification from breach of contract perpetuated by Pilipinas Shell, but also a full compensation for costs, expenses and efforts as well as all other claims relative to the installation of the Hydrogen Manufacturing Unit and the Liquid Carbon Dioxide Plant, including its obligation under the Subject Agreement and its early termination.

Therefore, the award of the Termination Fee is not only compensatory for the breach of the Subject Agreement, but at the same time, a settlement for an underlying payment for services rendered which payment has not yet been received. Ergo, the Termination Fee does not extricate from the purview of VAT as the same bears direct relevance to the taxpayer's course of trade or business.

In the same vein, the Termination Fee is subject to income tax, the same being compensation for the loss of anticipated profits. This is pursuant to Section 27 (A) of the Tax Code, as amended, which provides:

"SEC. 27. Rates of Income Tax on Domestic Corporations. —

(A) In General. — Except as otherwise provided in this Code, an income tax of twenty-five percent (25%) effective July 1, 2020 is hereby imposed upon the taxable income derived during each taxable year from all sources within and without the Philippines by every corporation, as defined in Section 22(B) of this Code and taxable under this Title as a corporation, organized in, or existing under the laws of the Philippines."

The phrase "from whatever source derived" indicates a legislative policy to include all income not expressly exempted within the class of taxable income under our laws. The term "income" has been variously interpreted to mean "cash received or its equivalent," "the amount of money coming to a person within a specific time" or "something distinct from principal or capital." [1]

The definition of income is broad enough to include the Termination Fee consequent to the breach of the Subject Agreement, hence, subject to regular income tax.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

This refers to your request, on behalf of SHARE TREATS INNOVATION CORPORATION ("STIC"), for a ruling regarding its status as a taxpayer and the effects of its transactions for taxation purposes. EcTCAD

As represented, STIC is a domestic corporation registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) with Registration No. CS201718831 dated June 8, 2017, with primary purpose "to engage in Information Technology enable services such as but not limited to computer programming and software development," and with secondary purpose, among others, to engage in, conduct, and carry, on the business of acquiring, buying, importing, selling, holding, or otherwise disposing of and dealing with, insofar as may be permitted by law, aggregate brand vouchers, other goods, wares, merchandise and commodities of all kinds, and products, natural or artificial, of the Philippines or other countries, which are or may become articles of commerce, primarily through electronic commercial means without engaging in retail trade. It is likewise registered with the Bureau of Internal Revenue under Certificate of Registration No. OCN: 050RC20200000000987 originally dated June 28, 2017.

STIC offers a suite of platforms designated to digitize traditional gifting and rewarding and which involves the following features:

a. STIC enters into Marketing or Promotional Agreements with various "Merchants" wherein STIC will purchase electronic gift certificates (eGCs) for distribution;

b. eGCs include a monetary value that could be spent for any product or service at specific Merchants;

c. Once STIC purchases the eGCs, either the STIC or the Merchant will generate unique eGC codes to be made available to its Clients;

i. STIC advances the payment for the GCs to the Merchants and STIC records this as a prepaid expense. Here is a pro-forma entry for the prepayment: SDHTEC

Prepaid expense

xxx

Cash in bank

xxx

d. Clients purchase eGCs from STIC's online platform. A pro-forma entry in STIC's books for the sale of eGCs is as follows:

Accounts receivable

xxx

Prepaid taxes (withholding tax)

xxx

Prepaid expenses

xxx

Revenue

xxx

Output tax

xxx

STIC credits the value of the eGCs from the prepaid expense account previously established. Revenue is recognized for STIC's service fees for facilitation or administration and/or marketing efforts or commission.

e. STIC issues the following documents to the Clients:

i. Acknowledgment receipt — for the receipt of the value of the eGC representing the amount credited to STIC's prepaid expense account.

ii. Official receipt — representing the service fee billed to STIC's Clients.

f. Clients may be designated as individual customers or corporate customers;

i. Upon purchase of an eGC by an individual, the Client or designated recipient of the eGC shall be notified with an eGC code via electronic mail or short messaging service (SMS);

ii. For corporate Client, STIC provides the platform where the corporate Clients can send the eGC codes to their recipients.

g. The Clients or their designated recipient use the eGC codes to acquire goods or services from the Merchant by presenting the code to the cashier in participating stores or to the online website store or platform of the Merchant;

h. For sale of goods and services through the redemption of eGCs, the Merchant issues a corresponding value-added tax (VAT)-official receipt or sales invoice to the eGC Client or authorized representative and accounts for corresponding taxes thereto. HSAcaE

In view of the foregoing representations, STIC requests for confirmation of the following:

1. The proceeds from the issuance of eGCs from Clients to STIC is not a taxable income on the part of STIC as STIC merely offsets them to prepayments made to the Merchant to whom the Client will redeem the eGCs. Accordingly, the same is not subject to expanded withholding taxes (EWT);

2. STIC's issuance of eGCs to Clients is exempt from VAT and as such, the issuance of an acknowledgement receipt is proper, not being a sale of goods or service contemplated under the existing laws, rules and regulations on VAT; and

3. STIC shall be subject to 12% VAT and be required to issue VAT official receipts on the amount it receives from its Clients for the service fees where eGCs were utilized for facilitation or administration and/or marketing efforts or commission.

In reply, we take note of the following, based on your representations:

1. Based on item (a.) of the representations above, STIC claims that it enters into Marketing or Promotional Agreements with various "Merchants," and yet STIC will purchase eGCs for distribution. If the service that STIC renders to its Merchants is for marketing or promotion, then the ownership of the eGCs still belongs to the Merchants; thus, there is no reason for STIC to purchase the eGCs and to advance payment to the Merchants. The pro-forma entry clearly shows that it is one of purchase, as the debit entry is a "pre-paid expense."

Apparently, STIC takes ownership of the eGCs once it advances payment of the eGCs to the Merchants. In fact, per item (c.) of the representations, the unique eGC codes can only be generated after STIC purchases the eGCs.

2. Based on item (e.) of the representations, STIC issues official receipts for the amount representing the service fee it bills to its Clients, which is not consistent with the "Marketing or Promotional" feature/activity it allegedly performs for the Merchants.

Apparently, it is STIC's Clients, and not the Merchants, which pay for STIC's services in the form of service fees.

Based on STIC's representations therefore, it is apparent that STIC purchases the eGCs from the Merchants, takes ownership of the eGCs; sells the eGCs to its Clients; and charges its Clients a service fee. AScHCD

Hence, the Bureau shall base its ruling on such representations. However, we also take notice of Republic Act (RA) No. 10962 [1] of the "Gift Check Act of 2017," Section 2 of which states the nature of gift certificates or gift checks as follows:

"Towards this end, the State, through the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), recognizes that a gift check represents value held in trust by the issuer thereof on behalf of its beneficiary or bearer and that consumers must not be unduly deprived of the value of their money."

Applying the foregoing in the instant case, we have the following ruling:

The proceeds from STIC's Clients, for the face value of the eGCs issued, represent value held in trust by the issuer thereof (i.e., the Merchant) on behalf of its beneficiary or bearer (i.e., the Clients) until such time when the beneficiary or bearer will redeem the eGCs. Therefore, such proceeds do not constitute taxable income of STIC, as contemplated in Section 27 (A) of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997, as amended ("Tax Code").

We reiterate BIR Ruling No. 242-18 dated February 21, 2018, quoting the case of Commissioner of Internal Revenue vs. Tour Specialists, Inc., [2] citing the case of Commissioner of Internal Revenue vs. Manila Jockey Club, Inc., [3] where the Supreme Court declared that:

"Gross receipts subject to tax under the Tax Code do not include monies or receipts entrusted to the taxpayer which do not belong to them and do not redound to the taxpayer's benefit and it is not necessary that there must be a law or regulation which would exempt such monies and receipts within the meaning of gross receipts under the Tax Code."

In the foregoing case, the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Tax Appeals which excluded from the gross receipts of a local travel agency amounts received by the latter from foreign tourist agencies which form part of the package fee paid by the tourists but were intended or earmarked for hotel room accommodations and accordingly paid by the local travel agency to the hotels. In said case, the Court found that the hotel charges paid by the local travel agency were paid out of funds entrusted to it by the foreign tour correspondent agency. As such, the said receipts never belonged to the local travel agency, but only formed sums for payment to the hotels, without any portion thereof being diverted to its own fund.

Since the proceeds from the Clients for the face value of the eGCs do not constitute taxable income on the part of STIC, accordingly, such proceeds are not subject to EWT. [4]

Even if, technically, STIC has already purchased the eGCs from the Merchants, as explained previously, STIC may still be considered a "beneficiary or bearer" of the eGCs that have not been sold to any Clients yet, which means that the face value of such eGCs do not represent a sale but a value held in trust by the Merchants in favor of STIC. HESIcT

For the proceeds received by STIC from its Clients for the face value of the eGCs, since they do not fall within the purview of the term taxable income, nor are they considered payment for goods sold by STIC, nor considered compensation for services rendered by STIC, such proceeds are not considered as sale of goods or service as contemplated under Section 105 of the Tax Code, and other rules and regulations related to VAT. As such, the proceeds for the face value of the eGCs are not subject to VAT; thus, the issuance of an acknowledgement receipt for such proceeds is proper.

As for the proceeds received by STIC from its Clients pertaining to the service fees for the facilitation or administration and/or marketing efforts or commission, being considered income on the part of STIC, STIC shall be subject to 12% VAT and shall be required to issue VAT official receipts on such amount. The service fees are also subject to EWT on the part of the Clients, as applicable.

However, for unused or unspent eGC, STIC shall recognize revenue therefor, which shall be subject to ordinary corporate income tax, and, commission, if any, paid by STIC to merchants for every eGC spent in their stores shall be subject to income tax and to creditable income tax and VAT.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request on behalf of your client Agros Trofi Corporation ("Agros Trofi") doing business under the name of "Rocko's Herb-Roasted Chicken" for confirmation that the sale of roasted chicken is exempt from value-added tax (VAT). aScITE

It is represented that Agros Trofi is a domestic corporation engaged in the sale of herb-roasted chicken on a take-out basis only. It does not maintain any facility by which the said roasted chicken is offered to customers who would dine-in.

In reply, please be informed that Section 109 (1) (A) of the National Internal Revenue Code (Tax Code) of 1997, as amended, provides:

"SEC. 109. Exempt Transactions — (1) Subject to the provisions of Subsection (2) hereof, the following transactions shall be exempt from the value-added tax:

(A) Sale or importation of agricultural and marine food products in their original state, livestock and poultry of a kind generally used as, or yielding or producing foods for human consumption; and breeding stock and genetic materials therefor.

Products classified under this paragraph shall be considered in their original state even if they have undergone the simple processes of preparation or preservation for the market such as freezing, drying, salting, broiling, roasting, smoking or stripping. Polished and/or husked rice, corn grits, raw cane sugar and molasses, ordinary salt, and copra shall be considered in their original state; x x x" (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

In relation thereto, Section 4.109-1 (B) (1) (a) of Revenue Regulations (RR) No. 16-2005, as amended provides: DETACa

"SECTION 4.109-1. VAT-Exempt Transactions. —

xxx xxx xxx

(B) Exempt transactions. —

(1) Subject to the provisions of Sec. 4.109-2 hereof, the following transactions shall be exempt from VAT:

(a) Sale or importation of agricultural and marine food products in their original state, livestock and poultry of a kind generally used as, or yielding or producing foods for human consumption; and breeding stock and genetic materials therefor

xxx xxx xxx

Meat, fruit, fish, vegetables and other agricultural and marine food products classified under this paragraph shall be considered in their original state even if they have undergone the simple processes of preparation or preservation for the market, such as freezing, drying, salting, broiling, roasting, smoking or stripping, including those using advanced technological means of packaging, such as shrink wrapping in plastics, vacuum packing, tetra-pack, and other similar packaging methods.

xxx xxx xxx" (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

It is worth noting that the records of the Bicameral Conference Committee reveal the pragmatic reason underlying the exemption, viz.:

"MR. DAMASING: More or less, your Honor, can you give us just few example that would show that the House is more receptive to the cry of the poor people rather than the Senate.

MR. JAVIER: Well, for example, your Honor, one is we were able to get a presumptive tax credit items — food items which are being purchased mostly by our workers. Like, sardines, canned fish, milk, sugar and then cooking oil. Then another, would be — we refined the definition of agricultural products. For example, it now included roasting and broiling. So, if our worker who goes home at night because of traffic stops at ANDOK'S LECHON, and buys roasted chicken on a take-out basis NO VAT will be imposed on his purchase of that roasted chicken" (Emphasis and underscoring supplied)

From the forgoing, this Office hereby confirms that Agros Trofi's sale of chicken as a food product, which had undergone the simple process of roasting, on a take-out basis, is covered by the VAT-exemption by express provision of the law.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be disclosed that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Details.Details:
BIR Ruling No. 123-2013

Norteam Shipping Services, Inc.
Suite 201, ITC Building
337 Sen. Gil Puyat Avenue, Makati City

Attention: Julito B. Quiban, Jr.

President

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request that Norteam Shipping Service, Inc. ("NSSI") be allowed to record the unclaimed/denied value-added tax ("VAT") refund claim as "miscellaneous expense" for income tax purposes. HTcADC

It is represented that NSSI has filed a claim for VAT refund representing unutilized input VAT attributable to zero-rated sales pursuant to Section 112 (A) of the National Internal Revenue Code ("Tax Code") of 1997, as amended. Subsequently, the claim for VAT refund was denied for lack of factual and legal basis.

NSSI expressed that it no longer intends to pursue a judicial appeal with the Court of Tax Appeals ("CTA") due to high cost that may be incurred. Instead, NSSI is requesting that it be allowed to record the unclaimed/denied claim for VAT refund as "miscellaneous expense" for income tax purposes, citing the case of Commissioner of Internal Revenue vs. Maersk Global Service Center (Philippines) Ltd. (CTA Case EB 1786, June 13, 2019), wherein the CTA En Banc allowed the previously denied claim VAT refund to be deducted as expenses from gross income.

In reply, please be informed that Revenue Memorandum Circular ("RMC") No. 57-2013 previously clarified the issues concerning the recovery of unutilized creditable input taxes attributable to VAT zero-rated sales, to wit:

"[T]hat unutilized creditable input taxes attributable to zero-rated sales can only be recovered through the application for refund or tax credit. Nowhere in the Tax Code can we find a specific provision expressly providing for another mode of recovering unapplied input taxes, particularly your proposition that unapplied input taxes may be treated outright as deductible expense for income tax purposes. x x x" (Underscoring supplied)

Moreover, the Supreme Court in the case of United Coconut Planters Bank vs. Sps. Uy, G.R. No. 204039, January 10, 2018, explained that Stare Decisis applies only to cases decided by the Supreme Court, to wit:

"In other words, the doctrine of stare decisis becomes operative only when judicial precedents are set by pronouncements of this Court to the exclusion of lower courts. It is true regardless whether the decisions of the lower courts are logically or legally sound as only decisions issued by this Court become part of the legal system. At the most, decisions of lower courts only have a persuasive effect." CAIHTE

The Supreme Court clearly established that the decision of lower courts, such as the CTA, is not a binding precedent considering that judicial precedents are only set by pronouncements of the Supreme Court to the exclusion of lower courts.

Accordingly, in the absence of a Supreme Court ruling allowing the same, RMC No. 57-2013 shall be enforced, and that the unutilized creditable input taxes attributable to zero-rated sales can only be recovered through the application for refund or tax credit.

Therefore, in view of the foregoing, this Office hereby denies the request of NSSI to claim the unutilized creditable input taxes attributable to VAT zero-rated sales as deduction for income tax purposes.

Please be guided accordingly.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue

Sections 131, 134 & 141 of the Tax Code of 1997, as amended;
Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 24-2023; BIR Ruling Nos. 700-19 and 040-00

Philippine Economic Zone Authority
10th Floor, Double Dragon Center West Building
DID Meridian Park, Macapagal Avenue, Pasay City

Attention: Mr. Tereso O. Panga

Deputy Director General for Policy and Planning

Gentlemen :

This refers to your request, referred to in this Office by the Large Taxpayers Service (LTS), for exemption from Excise Tax for the importation of Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol 96%), a raw material used in the production operations of Landel Logistics Corporation (LLC)'s Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA)-registered Ecozone Export Enterprise (EEE) clients. DETACa

Documents submitted show that LLC is a PEZA-registered Ecozone Logistics Service Enterprise (ELSE) at the Light Industry & Science Park III-Special Economic Zone with Certificate of Registration No. 05-06-F dated February 07 2005; and that PEZA has issued a certification dated April 18, 2023 in favor of LLC allowing the latter to engage in warehousing/logistics support services, particularly importation, storage, safekeeping of goods for subsequent sale, transfer or disposition to PEZA/BOI-registered export enterprises and to export enterprises operating at the Clark and Subic Economic Zones.

Hence, this request.

At the outset, Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 24-2023 in relation to BOI Memorandum Circular No. 2023-001 clarifies that Ecozone Logistics Service Enterprise (ELSE), such as LLC, is considered as an export enterprise as defined under Republic Act (RA) No. 11534 or the CREATE Act, it being engaged in activities in support to exporters. It thus follows that LLC is exempt from VAT on importation of goods for subsequent transfer directly to PEZA-registered export enterprise, for direct export.

On the issue of excise tax relative to ethyl alcohol, please be informed of the following provisions of the National Internal Revenue Code of 1997 (Tax Code), as amended, which may be applicable in the instant case, to wit: aDSIHc

"SEC. 141. Distilled Spirits. — On distilled spirits, subject to the provisions of Section 133 of this Code, an excise tax shall be levied, assessed and collected based on the following schedules:

xxx xxx xxx

(B) Effective on January 1, 2021

(1) An ad valorem tax equivalent to twenty percent (22%) [n] of the net retail price (excluding the excise tax and the value-added tax) per proof; and

(2) In addition to the ad valorem tax herein imposed, a specific tax of Twenty pesos (P47.00) [n] per proof liter.

xxx xxx xxx

(F) In addition to the ad valorem tax herein imposed, the specific tax imposed under this Section shall be increased by six percent (6%) every year thereafter, effective on January 1, 2025, through revenue regulations issued by the Secretary of Finance.

xxx xxx xxx

This tax shall be proportionally increased for any strength of the spirits taxed over proof spirits, and the tax shall attach to this substance as soon as it is in existence as such, whether it be subsequently separated as pure or impure spirits, or transformed into any other substance either in the process of original production or by any subsequent process.

'Spirits or distilled spirits' is the substance known as ethyl alcohol, ethanol or spirits of wine, including all dilutions, purifications and mixtures thereof from whatever source, by whatever process produced, and shall include whisky, brandy, rum, gin and vodka, and other similar products or mixtures."

Section 131 of the same Code provides for the payment of excise taxes on imported articles, to wit:

"SEC. 131. Payment of Excise Taxes on Imported Articles. —

xxx xxx xxx

(B) Rate and Basis of the Excise Tax on Imported Articles. — Unless otherwise specified, imported articles shall be subject to the same rates and basis of excise taxes applicable to locally manufactured articles."

Based thereon, imported spirits or distilled spirits are subject to an excise tax at the same rates and basis applicable to similar products locally manufactured. While Section 141 considered ethyl alcohol as substance of spirits or distilled spirits, it can be clearly gleaned that the law pertains to those products of ethyl alcohol which are fit for human consumption.

On the other hand, Section 134, Chapter II of the Tax Code, as amended, provides for the exemption or conditional tax-free removal of Domestic Denatured Alcohol, to wit: HEITAD

"CHAPTER II

EXEMPTION OR CONDITIONAL TAX-FREE REMOVAL OF CERTAIN ARTICLES

xxx xxx xxx

"SEC. 134. Domestic Denatured Alcohol. — Domestic alcohol of not less than one hundred eighty degrees (180º) proof (ninety percent (90%) absolute alcohol) shall, when suitably denatured and rendered unfit for oral intake, be exempt from the excise tax prescribed in Section 141: Provided, however, That such denatured alcohol shall be subject to tax under Section 106 (A) of this Code: Provided, further, That if such alcohol is to be used for motive power, it shall be taxed under Section 148 (d) of this Code: Provided, finally, That any alcohol, previously rendered unfit for oral intake after denaturing but subsequently rendered fit for oral intake after undergoing fermentation, dilution, purification, mixture or any other similar process shall be taxed under Section 141 of this Code and such tax shall be paid by the person in possession of such reprocessed spirits."

Evidently, when the domestic alcohol falls under the purview of Section 134 hereof, such as: (1) the domestic alcohol is not less than 180º proof or 90% absolute alcohol, (2) the same is suitably denatured; and (3) it is rendered unfit for oral intake, no excise tax may be imposed thereon. However, when such denatured alcohol is to be used for motive power, it shall be taxed under Section 148 (D) of the Tax Code, as amended, or when any alcohol previously rendered unfit for oral intake or after denaturing but subsequently rendered fit for oral intake after undergoing fermentation, dilution, purification, mixture or any other similar process shall be taxed under Section 141 of the Tax Code, as amended.

In summary, to be entitled to the excise tax exemption under Section 134, the following requisites must be present:

1) That the domestic alcohol is not less than 180º proof or 90% absolute alcohol;

2) That the same is suitably denatured; and

3) That it is rendered unfit for oral intake.

In the instant case, since it clearly shows that the subject goods (alcohol) were imported and not domestically manufactured/acquired, it is irrelevant to ascertain the degree of proof or the rate of the alcohol content containing the product. Section 134 of the Tax Code, as amended, categorically pertains to domestic alcohol and nothing in the said code mentioned about imported alcohol. Nevertheless, in case where the said product is to be used for motive power or subsequently rendered fit for oral intake, through fermentation, dilution, purification, mixture or any other similar process, it shall be taxed under Section 148 (D) and Section 141, respectively, of the Tax Code, as amended, pursuant to the provision of Section 131 (B) of the same code. ATICcS

In view of all the foregoing, this Office hereby holds that the request for exemption from the imposition of Excise Tax on importation by Landel Logistics Corporation of Ethyl Alcohol is hereby denied for lack of legal basis.

This ruling is being issued on the basis of the foregoing facts as represented. However, if upon investigation, it will be ascertained that the facts are different, then this ruling shall be considered null and void.

Very truly yours,

(SGD.) ROMEO D. LUMAGUI, JR.
Commissioner of Internal Revenue
